items.title: The pioneering coding tricks that built Doom and Quake
items.summary: Ryan chats with John Romero, creator of the WAD file and the video game Doom, about the self-modifying code and blitting techniques that made Wolfenstein run so fast on early PCs, the mod-friendly architecture that turned Doom into a cultural phenomenon, and why the raw creative problem-solving of Quake proves that human ideas will always beat AI coding agents.

items.title: 90% of Claude Code Is Written by Claude — Here's How the Team Verifies Every Change
items.summary: On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of the code — around 90% — is written and reviewed by Claude itself. At that scale, the question is no longer whether an agent can write code. It's whether an agent can prove its code works. That's the subject of a new post from Anthropic's Claude.dev blog, "How the Claude Code team thinks about verification," written by Addy Osmani and published on November 16. The core argument is simple: verification loops are what let you delegate more work to agents. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. Why verification beats better prompting In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude's work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop — with the largest gains on the hardest problems. The reason is economic. Things that used to be expensive to verify — tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs — are now cheap to ask an agent to produce. And once generated, those tests run as software, so they can be executed frequently without burning many additional tokens. The loop closes when results feed back into the agent's behavior. If an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, the team adds a hook or a more explicit rule in CLAUDE.md to stop it happening again. Verification isn't just a gate; it's how the agent gets better at the task. The three tests worth investing in Not all tests are equal, and the post is blunt about the failure modes: flaky tests train the agent to re-run tests instead of fixing code, and slow tests mean fewer tests per batch, which makes bugs harder to pinpoint. Heavier tests belong before the change is committed. Within that frame, three types earn their keep. End-to-end tests. If you focus on one type, pick this one. E2E tests describe real user flows — add an item to a cart, check out, reach the confirmation page. They are hard to fool: either the whole feature works or it doesn't. And unlike a unit test that just says "timeout after 30 seconds," an E2E failure gives you a step trace, a screenshot, and a description of what broke. Unit tests are faster and less flaky, but you can pass them all and still ship a broken feature, because neither the agent nor the test understood the full task. Property tests. Most tests are written around what you thought might go wrong. Property tests hunt the edge cases people tend to miss — exactly where agents often fail. You write a statement you think can't fail (round-trip encoding, an invariant like "account balance can never become negative," idempotency, equivalence with a naive implementation), then let a library — fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust — generate thousands of inputs trying to prove it wrong. The edge cases come from the library, not from the agent that wrote the original code, so they don't share its blind spots. They're especially useful in rewrites, where the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source of truth. Differential tests. When functionality is expected to stay the same — a large-scale migration, for example — run the old system and the new system on the same inputs and compare. Any difference is a bug or a breaking change. The trick is using randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic, normalizing irrelevant differences like whitespace, and keeping a list of approved changes for places where the new environment is supposed to differ. How the team applies verification in practice The post then gets specific about how the Claude Code team runs its own workflow: Verification means running the change. Running the app end to end matters more than tests. Claude tests the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would — the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or a locally running service for backend work. The team codifies how to boot the simulator or run the app in a skill called verify , stored in the repo's .claude/skills/ folder, close to the relevant code. Claude knows to use it before committing. Then they invest in making that skill fast and reliable, iterating and stress-testing it, because it's the smoke test harness for everything. Failing tests escalate to a human. Nobody can read every change, so failures are the signal for what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human. Code owners write their own checks. The people who own the code write and refine the checks for it, until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so the reviewer doesn't have to work it out from the diff. Reliability checks trigger on the diff. The team maintains a 39-item reliability checklist, each item with a trigger readable from a diff, a check, and the incident or PR behind it. One example: "--resume loads old transcripts" — when session storage or message types change, the team asks whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won't have it. Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches, usually 3 to 10, so nobody has to memorize past outages. One reviewer, multiple rounds. The team doesn't improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers; tuning the primary reviewer beats adding a second, more expensive one. Instead they keep a REVIEW.md file describing what the reviewer should pay attention to for that code. Review rounds build on each other, each pass pointing at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It's cheaper, and it finds more. Changes can't modify their own checks. If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base or default branch — never from the pull request's changes. The rules that gate changes live on a branch the change can't touch. Reviews are also reserved for commits: a passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing. And cheap checks run first — Claude runs tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request, so it doesn't spend shared review and CI time on a bug it could have caught itself. New gates start in observe mode. Every commit is stamped with how it was verified — the stamp even includes "none," so unverified commits can be queried. A commit gate can block a commit if the session didn't include /code-review or /verify , with off, observe, and enforce modes. Observe mode logs what would have been blocked, so false positives can be reviewed before anyone is affected. Enforce mode blocks the commit, though any commit can explain in its message why it wasn't verified, and if commits have been blocked twice in a session, the next one is allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck. Test your checks on what actually matters. The team regularly reviews the reviewers, tracking how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that stayed clean. The Code Review team built a formal evaluation from past incidents and reverts: each example recreates the repo at the time of review with a one-sentence answer key for the bug, and only findings that correctly describe that bug score. Merged, stable changes serve as a control against over-flagging, and the tuning set is kept separate from the fixed test set. Recall is measured separately for raw findings, post-verification, and final review, so the team can see whether the system is losing bugs it already found. Importance is graded too — findings are tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a reviewer doesn't hold an author responsible for a bug that was already there. Finally, recall is tuned up only to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs. Turn misses into rules. The repo has two ways of converting a missed case into a rule. First, patterns are extracted from human code review comments and PR reverts: a candidate must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff, then three agents try to disprove it, and a human reviews and approves it in a PR. Second, three bug finders replay a PR associated with a known incident — if at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug, and missing it on a small diff is a gap worth writing into REVIEW.md . Flaky tests get the same treatment: Claude can't skip them, add sleeps, or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why. And rules need pruning — test suites, verification steps, and .md files only grow, so the team tidies them on a routine. The shift that matters The post's closing line reframes the whole job: once verification works, your work shifts from reading every diff to defining what "done" looks like and reviewing the evidence. That's what lets you run many Claudes at once. For teams adopting coding agents, the takeaway isn't "write more tests." It's that the verification layer is a system of its own — one that needs to be fast, honest, and out of reach of the changes it judges. Keep it close to the code it protects, grade it against the bugs that actually hurt, and write down the lesson every time it misses something, so it never misses the same thing twice. Source: Anthropic, "How the Claude Code team thinks about verification" (claude.dev, November 16, 2026).

items.title: Five monitoring checks every WordPress site needs (and the one plugin that cannot do them)
items.summary: Originally published on the Tenium blog . I'm the author of Tenium, an uptime monitor for agencies. WordPress fails in ways a basic uptime check does not see. The classic example: the database goes away, WordPress renders a tidy page that says "Error establishing a database connection", and returns it with HTTP 200 . Your monitor says everything is fine. Your client's customers see an error. Here are the five external checks we set up on every WordPress site, why each exists, and how to configure them. Together they make a standard set you can create in Tenium by hand or from a CSV; there is no one-click template. 1. Home page: status code plus keyword The home page check should require two things: a 2xx status and the presence of a phrase that only appears when the site rendered properly. The phrase does not have to be visible text. wp-content is a good default because every properly rendered WordPress page references assets under that path, while the database error page and most PHP fatal error pages do not. For shops, use a phrase from the real page: the store name in the footer, or the first product title. Also add a must not contain rule for Error establishing a database connection and Fatal error . That turns the common failure modes into explicit alerts with a useful message, instead of "keyword missing". Interval: 30 or 60 seconds. This is the one that pages you. 2. The login page /wp-login.php is where security plugins and WAFs misbehave. Wordfence rate-limits, a Cloudflare rule challenges everyone, a plugin update renames the login URL, or a hosting firewall blocks a country that includes your office. The site is up, but nobody can log in, including you, and the client's editor is the one who finds out. Monitor https://example.com/wp-login.php and expect a 200 with the keyword user_login . If you have moved the login URL, monitor the new one. Interval: 5 minutes is plenty. Caveat: a security plugin may block repeated requests to the login page. Allow-list the monitor's IPs or User-Agent in the plugin; see the Cloudflare guide for the pattern. 3. wp-cron heartbeat WordPress has no real cron. Scheduled posts, backups, WooCommerce stock syncs and plugin housekeeping all run from wp-cron.php , which is triggered by page visits. On a quiet site, or one where a developer disabled wp-cron without replacing it, scheduled jobs silently stop. The site looks healthy. Backups have not run for three months. The fix is a heartbeat monitor: a unique URL that expects a ping at least every N minutes. Heartbeat monitors start on the Starter plan. Create one in Tenium with a period of 15 minutes and a grace of 15 minutes, then drop this must-use plugin into wp-content/mu-plugins/tenium-heartbeat.php : php /* Plugin Name: Tenium heartbeat */ add_action ( 'init' , function ( ) { if ( ! wp_next_scheduled ( 'tenium_heartbeat' ) ) { wp_schedule_event ( time ( ) , 'hourly' , 'tenium_heartbeat' ) ; } } ) ; add_filter ( 'cron_schedules' , function ( $s ) { $s [ 'tenium_15' ] = [ 'interval' => 900 , 'display' => 'Every 15 minutes' ] ; return $s ; } ) ; add_action ( 'tenium_heartbeat' , function ( ) { wp_remote_get ( 'https://ping.tenium.app/h/YOUR_HEARTBEAT_ID' , [ 'timeout' => 5 , 'blocking' => false ] ) ; } ) ; Change 'hourly' to 'tenium_15' once the schedule is registered, or just leave it hourly with a 90-minute period. If wp-cron stops, the heartbeat goes quiet and you get an alert that says exactly that. Bonus: if you have replaced wp-cron with a real system cron ( */5 * * * * wp cron event run --due-now ), append && curl -fsS https://ping.tenium.app/h/YOUR_ID to that line instead. 4. SSL certificate expiry Let's Encrypt renews automatically until the day it does not: a changed DNS record, a closed port 80, a rate limit, a hosting migration. An external SSL monitor reads the certificate visitors actually see and alerts at 30, 14 and 3 days before expiry, plus immediately if the chain breaks or the hostname does not match. Every https monitor in Tenium records expiry as a side effect, so your home-page check already does this. A dedicated SSL monitor adds chain and issuer checks and shows a clear "61 days left" on the client's status page and monthly report. If you have ever had to recover an expired certificate on a Monday morning, you will not skip this one. 5. Domain expiry The domain is usually registered in the client's name, on a card that expired two years ago, with renewal emails going to a former employee. You find out when the home page is a parking page full of ads, and that is 100% downtime with reputational damage on top. A domain monitor checks the registry via RDAP or WHOIS weekly and alerts 60, 30, 14 and 7 days before expiry. It also flags nameserver changes and clientHold statuses. For an agency with forty client domains, the monitor list doubles as the renewal calendar, and the expiry date appears on each client's report, which tends to prompt the renewal conversation at the right time. The plugin that cannot do this Management plugins and services (ManageWP, MainWP, WP Umbrella and friends) are excellent at updates, backups and security scans from inside WordPress. They cannot tell you the site is down, because when the site is down the plugin is down with it. External monitoring and in-site management are complementary; use both, and put both on the care plan . Setting it up for forty sites In Tenium, paste the site URLs one per line or upload a CSV: each URL becomes an HTTP monitor, and you add the keyword, certificate and domain checks per site (or list them as extra CSV rows with a type and keyword). Forty sites is about 200 monitors, which fits the Pro plan at $29 a month. If you also want each site in its own client workspace, with a client login and a branded report sent on the 1st, that is the Agency plan at $59, which has room for 500 monitors. See WordPress monitoring for the details of each check. Related Each of the five checks has a page of its own: website monitoring , keyword monitoring , cron job monitoring , SSL monitoring and domain expiry monitoring . For the audience view, see monitoring for WordPress sites , and test any URL with the HTTP headers tool . Agencies can see how this scales in for agencies . If you look after many client sites, there is a free plan (50 monitors): https://tenium.app/?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=cross-post&utm_campaign=wordpress-checks

items.title: I Read 39 Arguments About Whether to Buy Something. One Field Predicted Every Verdict.
items.summary: Thirty-nine people argued for or against a purchase in front of strangers. I read all of them on 17 November 2026, then I read the JSON behind them. The JSON was more interesting than the arguments. The data source No browser, no scraping loop. WalletJury's front end loads cases from a public endpoint, so the audit is one request: GET https://walletjury.com/api/list?sort=new&limit=200&offset=0 39 cases came back with next: null . Null means no more pages, so it's the entire database rather than a sample — nothing filtered, nothing skipped, 29,402 bytes. Then we dumped every key on every case. Twenty-one keys. items.summary_html:
Thirty-nine people argued for or against a purchase in front of strangers. I read all of them on 17 November 2026, then I read the JSON behind them.

The JSON was more interesting than the arguments.

The data source

No browser, no scraping loop. WalletJury's front end loads cases from a public endpoint, so the audit is one request:

GET https://walletjury.com/api/list?sort=new&limit=200&offset=0

39 cases came back with next: null. Null means no more pages, so it's the entire database rather than a sample — nothing filtered, nothing skipped, 29,402 bytes.

Then we dumped every key on every case. Twenty-one keys.

What the fields actually contain
Field Filled Detail item 39/39 price 39/39 20 to 12,999 currency 39/39 USD 37, CNY 2 defense 39/39 32–375 characters, median 244 use 35/39 Daily 19, Weekly 8, Not sure 7, few times a year 1 afford 39/39 stretch 22, easily 10, not really 7 anon 39/39 all true authorName 0/39 never once hasImage 1/39 ai.lean 39/39 guilty 36, not guilty 3 ai.opinion 39/39 20–121 characters, median 52 outcome 0/39 the thing the product promises votes 46 total spread over 17 cases only replies 51 total

Twenty-one fields. Seven carry real variation: item, price, currency, defense, use, afford, and the AI's one-line opinion.

Three things I did not expect

One: 29 out of 29.

Every case where the poster picked "It's a stretch" (22 cases) or "Not really" (7 cases) came back Guilty. All 29, no exceptions across the whole database.

The only three Not Guilty verdicts sit inside the ten "Easily" cases. A 30% acquittal rate in one bucket, 0% in the other two.

Two: the vote count doesn't spread.

22 of 39 cases have zero votes. The other 17 have exactly 3 votes (12 cases) or exactly 2 (5 cases). Nothing between the two, nothing above three.

46 votes have been cast on this database, all inside those 17 cases, and every one landed on the same two numbers. That is not a distribution. That is a shape.

Three: three fields have never done anything.

authorName is empty on all 39. hasImage is true on one. outcome is null on all 39 — the field that would record what the jury decided.

Meanwhile afford, the field nobody thinks about, splits the dataset cleanly in two.

What we could not measure

Why. We can see the output and not the reasoning. Three readings fit this table:

The model reads afford and treats "I can easily afford this" as a reason to acquit. Or it ignores afford and reads the text — people who pick "easily" write differently than people who pick "stretch". Or it is self-selection: if you can afford the thing, you only post the genuinely borderline ones, and borderline cases get acquitted.

Telling those three apart needs controlled submissions. I am not going to post fake cases into a live product to get a prettier chart. The correlation is 29 for 29 and that is the whole of what I can defend.

We also didn't render the site in a browser for this piece. Everything above is the API payload, read as text.

A correction to our own notes

On 14 November I wrote that this site had 39 cases and 46 votes. It is 17 November and it is still 39 and 46.

I wrote that assuming the next pull would show movement. The newest case was created 23 October, 13:08 UTC, and nothing has arrived in the 25 days since. The first version should have said "unchanged since 23 October".

Disclosure

WalletJury is one of the sites we build and run. These numbers come from its own public endpoint, and nothing on the site was changed to produce them.

All 39 cases are public: walletjury.com

One open question

If you were building this, what do you do with a field that predicts the verdict 29 times out of 29?

Keep it, because it works. Drop it, because a jury that reads your bank balance before your argument is not a jury.

I genuinely don't know which answer is right.

items.title: How Yoast SEO Actually Works Under the Hood: A Technical Breakdown for WordPress Developers
items.summary:
Yoast SEO from a Systems Perspective Hầu hết tài liệu về Yoast SEO mô tả nó từ góc độ người dùng cuối: điền focus keyphrase, chờ đèn xanh, đăng bài. Nhưng với người xây dựng hoặc quản lý WordPress từ góc độ kỹ thuật, câu hỏi thực sự là: Yoast SEO làm gì với database, với DOM và với HTTP response — và làm thế nào nó có thể tích hợp hoặc xung đột với các hệ thống khác trong stack? Bài này phân tích cơ chế hoạt động thực tế của Yoast SEO: cách nó ghi metadata, tạo sitemap, inject schema, và những điểm cần chú ý khi triển khai trong môi trường có nhiều plugin hoặc automation pipeline. Lớp metadata: Yoast ghi dữ liệu đi đâu? Khi người dùng điền Tiêu đề SEO và Thẻ mô tả trong editor, Yoast không ghi vào bảng wp_posts . Toàn bộ metadata của Yoast lưu trong wp_postmeta với các key có prefix _yoast_wpseo_ : _yoast_wpseo_title — tiêu đề SEO tùy chỉnh (nếu khác template mặc định) _yoast_wpseo_metadesc — thẻ mô tả _yoast_wpseo_focuskw — focus keyphrase _yoast_wpseo_linkdex — điểm SEO (0–100) được tính toán và cache lại _yoast_wpseo_content_score — điểm khả năng đọc _yoast_wpseo_canonical — canonical URL tùy chỉnh nếu có _yoast_wpseo_meta-robots-noindex — chỉ thị noindex cụ thể cho bài Đây là điểm quan trọng khi xây dựng automation pipeline: nếu muốn ghi metadata hàng loạt qua code (ví dụ từ một AI content pipeline), anh em cần update_post_meta() vào đúng các key này, không phải ghi vào post title hay excerpt thông thường. Lưu ý khi dùng Yoast với WP-CLI hoặc REST API: Yoast có REST API endpoint riêng ( /wp/v2/yoast_head ) trả về rendered head HTML. Nhưng để ghi ngược lại metadata qua REST, cần đảm bảo schema của Yoast đã đăng ký field trong register_rest_field() — không phải mặc định của WordPress core. XML Sitemap: cơ chế tạo và cập nhật Yoast không tạo sitemap bằng cách generate file tĩnh vào filesystem. Thay vào đó, sitemap được serve động qua WordPress rewrite rules. Khi truy cập ten-website.com/sitemap_index.xml , WordPress xử lý request qua query var sitemap=1 và Yoast intercept để render XML output. Cấu trúc sitemap index phân cấp như sau: sitemap_index.xml — file index chứa danh sách sitemap con post-sitemap.xml — tất cả bài viết ( post_type=post ) page-sitemap.xml — tất cả trang ( post_type=page ) product-sitemap.xml — sản phẩm WooCommerce nếu có category-sitemap.xml , post_tag-sitemap.xml — taxonomy nếu được bật Sitemap được cache trong wp_options với key wpseo_sitemap_cache_validator . Cache bị invalidate mỗi khi post được publish, update hoặc delete — trigger qua WordPress hooks publish_post , save_post , delete_post . Ngoài ra, Yoast gửi XML-RPC ping đến Google và Bing mỗi khi sitemap được cập nhật — hành vi này có thể tắt bằng filter wpseo_allow_xml_sitemap_ping nếu không muốn. Schema injection: Yoast xây dựng JSON-LD thế nào? Yoast inject schema markup dưới dạng JSON-LD vào của mỗi trang. Thay vì schema phẳng, Yoast dùng Graph approach — một JSON-LD object duy nhất chứa nhiều entity liên kết nhau qua @id : { "@context" : "https://schema.org" , "@graph" : [ { "@type" : "WebPage" , "@id" : "https://example.com/post/#webpage" } , { "@type" : "Article" , "@id" : "https://example.com/post/#article" } , { "@type" : "Person" , "@id" : "https://example.com/#/schema/person/xxx" } , { "@type" : "Organization" , "@id" : "https://example.com/#organization" } , { "@type" : "WebSite" , "@id" : "https://example.com/#website" } ] } Graph approach này có ưu điểm là tránh khai báo entity trùng lặp và cho phép extend schema bằng cách thêm node mới vào graph thay vì sửa vào JSON đã có. Developer có thể hook vào wpseo_schema_graph_pieces để thêm custom schema piece hoặc modify piece đã có. Focus keyphrase analysis: scoring engine hoạt động ra sao? Hệ thống đèn màu của Yoast không phải heuristic đơn giản. Scoring engine chạy phía client (JavaScript) và phía server: Client-side analysis: Chạy trong browser khi người dùng đang soạn thảo. Yoast dùng thư viện JavaScript yoastseo (open source, có trên npm) để parse nội dung bài, tách câu, tính mật độ từ khóa và score từng assessment. Server-side scoring: Điểm cuối cùng được lưu vào _yoast_wpseo_linkdex và _yoast_wpseo_content_score khi save post. Mỗi assessment (keyword in title, keyword density, text length, image alt tags...) trả về một trong ba trạng thái: GOOD , OK , BAD — ánh xạ ra đèn xanh, cam, đỏ. Điểm tổng là weighted average của tất cả assessments. Điều quan trọng cần hiểu: scoring engine của Yoast là rule-based checklist, không phải mô hình ML . Nó không dự đoán khả năng xếp hạng — nó kiểm tra danh sách tiêu chí kỹ thuật xác định trước. Đèn xanh chỉ có nghĩa là bài pass checklist, không có nghĩa gì hơn. Khi nhìn vào hệ sinh thái plugin SEO WordPress rộng hơn — không chỉ Yoast — và cách các plugin như Rank Math hay Yoast so sánh với nhau ở tầng kiến trúc, bài viết phân tích toàn diện về Yoast SEO cung cấp bức tranh rõ hơn từ góc độ người triển khai. Xung đột plugin: vấn đề meta duplication Vấn đề phổ biến nhất khi Yoast xung đột với plugin khác là meta duplication : hai plugin cùng output tag hoặc cùng ghi og:title vào head, dẫn đến Google và Facebook đọc giá trị khác nhau.

Yoast handle việc này bằng cách:

  • Remove WordPress default title output: remove_action('wp_head', '_wp_render_title_tag', 1)
  • Remove theme title nếu theme dùng wp_title()

Rank Math và AIOSEO làm tương tự — đây là lý do không thể chạy song song hai plugin SEO: cả hai đều cố remove title của nhau và inject title của mình, kết quả là race condition không đoán được.

Cách kiểm tra xung đột: Inspect source HTML của bất kỳ trang nào, tìm trong xem có nhiều hơn một </code> tag hoặc nhiều <code>og:title</code> không. Nếu có, đang có plugin conflict.</p> <h2> Tích hợp Yoast với AI automation pipeline </h2> <p>Khi xây dựng pipeline tự động hóa nội dung trên WordPress — ví dụ AI viết bài và điền metadata hàng loạt — cần hiểu cách Yoast expect data được ghi vào.</p> <p>Có hai cách tiếp cận:</p> <h3> Cách 1: Ghi trực tiếp vào wp_postmeta </h3> <p>Dùng <code>update_post_meta($post_id, '_yoast_wpseo_title', $seo_title)</code> và <code>update_post_meta($post_id, '_yoast_wpseo_metadesc', $meta_desc)</code>. Cách này nhanh và không phụ thuộc vào Yoast API, nhưng cần đảm bảo format đúng (plain string, không có HTML tags).</p> <h3> Cách 2: Dùng Yoast REST API hoặc plugin-specific hooks </h3> <p>Yoast expose một số filter cho phép can thiệp vào quá trình render: <code>wpseo_title</code>, <code>wpseo_metadesc</code>, <code>wpseo_canonical</code>. Dùng các filter này nếu muốn dynamic override mà không lưu vào database.</p> <p>Onic AI SEO Automation xử lý vấn đề này bằng cách nhận diện Yoast tự động và ghi tiêu đề SEO, thẻ mô tả trực tiếp vào đúng trường của Yoast khi tối ưu hàng loạt — không cần can thiệp thủ công từng bài. Đây là ví dụ về cách một automation layer cần "biết" cấu trúc lưu trữ của từng plugin SEO để ghi đúng chỗ, thay vì ghi vào post title thông thường rồi bị Yoast override.</p> <h2> Sitemap và crawl budget: điểm cần lưu ý cho large-scale site </h2> <p>Với website có hàng trăm nghìn URL (WooCommerce lớn, news site), cần chú ý đến cách Yoast handle sitemap size:</p> <ul> <li>Yoast tự động split sitemap khi vượt quá 1,000 URLs mỗi file (configurable qua filter <code>wpseo_sitemap_entries_per_page</code>)</li> <li>Với large catalog, sitemap generation có thể gây timeout nếu chạy on-request. Nên pre-generate bằng WP-CLI: <code>wp yoast index --reindex</code> </li> <li>Cân nhắc exclude post types không cần index (custom post type nội bộ, revision logs) khỏi sitemap qua Yoast Settings để giảm crawl budget lãng phí</li> </ul> <h2> Kết luận: Yoast SEO trong kiến trúc WordPress </h2> <p>Yoast SEO là một metadata management layer đặt trên WordPress core — không phải một công cụ "magic SEO". Hiểu cơ chế lưu trữ trong <code>wp_postmeta</code>, cách sitemap được serve động qua rewrite rules, Graph schema approach và scoring engine rule-based giúp developer tích hợp đúng, debug nhanh hơn và xây dựng automation pipeline không phá vỡ dữ liệu hiện có.</p> <p>Khi kết hợp Yoast với AI automation pipeline, điểm mấu chốt là pipeline cần biết Yoast lưu metadata đi đâu (<code>_yoast_wpseo_*</code> keys trong <code>wp_postmeta</code>) và ghi vào đúng chỗ — đây là sự khác biệt giữa automation hoạt động đúng và automation tạo ra dữ liệu không nhất quán.</p> <p>Bài gốc: <a href="https://onic.vn/kien-thuc/yoast-seo/" rel="noopener noreferrer">https://onic.vn/kien-thuc/yoast-seo/</a></p>

items.title: Fix a washed-out MP4 without re-encoding: rewrite the range tag in both places
items.summary: Picture a ticket that says "the clip I uploaded looks foggy, the black parts are grey". When you run a product alone, you want that ticket closed in ten minutes, not a weekend spent on the transcode step. If the file is H.264 and only the range tag is wrong, re-encoding is unnecessary. A single ffmpeg command with -c copy rewrites the tag, leaves every compressed frame alone, and the blacks come back. The catch is that an MP4 stores that tag in two places, and the shortest version of the fix only touches one of them. Grey blacks mean limited pixels tagged as full The numbers below come from a self-made test pattern, not a customer clip: a 0–255 gray ramp on top and nine flat patches at 0, 8, 16, 64, 128, 192, 235, 247 and 255, encoded as 3 seconds of 8-bit H.264 (CRF 10, BT.709) on an Apple silicon Mac with ffmpeg, one run per variant. When pixels that only use Y 16–235 are tagged pc (full range), the decoder skips the stretch, and the nine patches come out as 16 / 23 / 30 / 71 / 126 / 181 / 218 / 228 / 235. Black never gets below 16, white stops at 235, and every patch in between is pulled toward the middle. That is the foggy look a user would describe. The opposite mistake looks nothing like it: full-range pixels tagged tv decode with 0–16 (17 levels) all flattened to 0 and 235–255 (21 levels) all pushed to 255. Nobody calls that washed out, which helps when all you have is a user's sentence. The direction matters before you touch the file, because the fix in the next section turns a correct full-range file into exactly that crushed version. So the first check is the real Y range, not the tag. On the washed-out test file, ffmpeg's signalstats filter reported YMIN 16 and YMAX 235 while ffprobe said pc , so the tag is wrong and the pixels are fine. One command rewrites both tags The command is ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -bsf:v h264_metadata=video_full_range_flag=0 -color_range tv out.mp4 . The h264_metadata bitstream filter flips the video_full_range_flag in the VUI, the flag the H.264 stream itself carries. The -color_range tv option changes what the MP4 muxer writes into the colr box, the container-level copy. -c copy means no decode and no encode, so there is no generation loss. After the rewrite, ffprobe reported pix_fmt=yuv420p and color_range=tv , and the patches decoded back to 0 for black, 128 for mid gray and 255 for white. The filter alone leaves the container saying pc The tempting shortcut is the bitstream filter alone, since decoders read that flag. In this test they did: a file with a tv bitstream flag and a pc container tag decoded exactly like the fully consistent tv file, both through ffmpeg and through a element in desktop Chromium drawn to a canvas, and the two paths differed by at most 1 on any patch. The mirror case held too: a pc bitstream flag under a tv container tag decoded just as grey as the fully mis-tagged file, so on these two paths a container-only fix would not help. So why bother with both? Because ffprobe -show_streams reports the container value, and -show_frames reports the bitstream value. After a filter-only fix, the first one still prints pc . If your upload validator checks with -show_streams , the fixed file looks broken and may get "fixed" back. The second reason is a guess, not a measurement: QuickTime, VLC, Safari, phone galleries and chat apps were not part of this test, and I don't know whether any of them prefers colr over the VUI. Writing the same value in both places makes that question irrelevant. Fix the step that wrote the tag Patching the file closes the ticket. The real bug is the step that produced limited pixels with a full-range tag, and the cheap way to catch it is a check in the upload path: read the frame-level tag with -show_frames , read YMIN and YMAX with signalstats , and flag any file tagged pc whose luma never leaves 16–235. I would not auto-fix on that rule, because a dim, low-contrast clip that really is full range can sit inside 16–235 too, so a flagged file still deserves a human look. HEVC was outside this test; h264_metadata only covers H.264. To see what a compressor ought to hand back, I use ImgIng https://imging.ai/ , a browser-based video compressor. In this test it got a full-range copy of the same gray pattern on its "visually near-lossless" preset in a desktop browser. One caveat: on a 3-second still pattern the result came out larger than the input, so ImgIng did not adopt it automatically; the readings below come from the candidate saved by hand and say something about tags, not final quality. It did not keep full range. The output came back as limited range, correctly tagged tv , and decoded to 0 / 255 for H.265 and 2 / 254 for H.264, with no grey floor and no clipping. One self-made sample, one run, but it gave me a target for my own pipeline: convert when you have to, tag what you actually wrote, and check the tag against the pixels before a user does it for you.

HEVC was outside this test; h264_metadata only covers H.264.

To see what a compressor ought to hand back, I use ImgIng https://imging.ai/ , a browser-based video compressor. In this test it got a full-range copy of the same gray pattern on its "visually near-lossless" preset in a desktop browser. One caveat: on a 3-second still pattern the result came out larger than the input, so ImgIng did not adopt it automatically; the readings below come from the candidate saved by hand and say something about tags, not final quality. It did not keep full range. The output came back as limited range, correctly tagged tv, and decoded to 0 / 255 for H.265 and 2 / 254 for H.264, with no grey floor and no clipping. One self-made sample, one run, but it gave me a target for my own pipeline: convert when you have to, tag what you actually wrote, and check the tag against the pixels before a user does it for you.

items.title: Let AI Trade with a Different Kind of Candlestick: A Complete Strategy Development and Iteration Loop with Your Own Agent
items.summary: A quiet fifteen minutes and fifteen minutes of suddenly surging volume each appear as a single fifteen-minute candlestick on a conventional chart. Yet the amount of trading activity within those two periods can be very different. What happens if we let trading volume determine when a bar closes, then use those bars to identify price breakouts? This time, we will work through a complete example using a “Volume Clock Breakout” strategy: give the idea to our own AI assistant, have it write the program, read backtest results, inspect runtime logs, and then make changes based on the evidence. Along the way, we need to answer a specific question: does observing the market at a different pace actually improve trading? In the previous article, we connected this development workflow using the Extended API and a strategy synchronization code. Here, we keep the same framework but switch to FMZ's MCP interface. We will hand tasks to the Agent step by step, working through connection setup, development and testing, and runtime inspections. 1. First, Distinguish Who Writes the Code from Who Executes the Trades An Agent is an AI assistant that can read and write files, call tools, and work through a sequence of tasks. MCP supplies the platform's tools and parameter descriptions, allowing the Agent to understand how to read strategies, save versions, submit backtests, and query results. Propose a trading idea ↓ The Agent writes the strategy and tests ↓ Via MCP The platform runs the backtest and returns results and logs ↓ The Agent analyzes the evidence, makes changes, and validates again After deployment, the strategy program processes market data and calculates signals, while the FMZ Docker runs the program and connects to the exchange. Each trade follows rules written in advance. The Agent handles research, development, and inspection, and can also carry out updates within an explicitly defined scope of operations. Periodic inspections also require the client or an external scheduler to wake the Agent. MCP supplies the tools; the scheduler initiates inspections at the specified times. The local project stores the source code, experiment configurations, and records. This is what makes it possible to trace an error log to the version that is running, and to associate a backtest with the rules and parameters used at the time. In plain language: The strategy running as a live trading instance on FMZ is the program that does the trading. The AI Agent handles strategy development, testing, iteration, evaluation, review, and supervision of that instance. 2. Connect Your Own AI and Complete a Read Operation First Open the FMZ homepage, find “Put FMZ in the hands of your own AI agent,” and click “Copy setup instructions.” Give the instructions to your assistant and specify the scope for this round: Read https://www.fmz.com/agent/setup.md, then connect to FMZ Quant. Request all permissions for this round. After connecting, list the available tools, verify the permissions, and complete one read-only query. Do not create or start any running instances yet. Let the Agent learn how to connect, as shown below: Click the authorization link provided by the Agent: According to the official setup guide, the Agent provides a confirmation link after requesting authorization. You sign in through your browser, review the permissions, and authorize access; the Agent then finishes configuring the connection. If you already have a connection, you can first check whether it works. The tool counts shown in the screenshots are illustrative; use the actual tool list returned after connecting. A successful connection is established by tools returning data successfully, not merely by the assistant saying “Setup is complete.” The read, backtest, and write permissions cover reading, backtesting, and saving changes, respectively. Creating, starting, or stopping instances later requires trade permission, along with explicit identification of the instance, Docker, and exchange object. Exchange API keys are configured on the platform's website; the Agent uses the IDs of objects that have already been configured. Permissions can be adjusted on the API Key management page. For this round, create a separate strategy. During connection setup, save a record of one successful query and the available tool scope. All subsequent development will use the same strategy ID. 3. Turn the Volume Clock into a Reproducible Experiment First, Explain Why the Idea Is Worth Testing A conventional fifteen-minute bar closes when its time is up. A volume bar accumulates trading volume and closes when it reaches a target. Suppose a bar has a target of 1,000 volume units: at 50 units traded per minute, it takes twenty minutes to complete; at 250 units per minute, it takes four minutes. This simply illustrates the mechanism. The actual target is calculated from historical data. Our hypothesis is that updating the observation interval more quickly when trading activity is concentrated may help identify breakouts sooner. We also need to consider the opposite possibility: the price may already have moved a long way by the time volume surges, faster bar formation may produce more false breakouts, and any additional returns may fall short of covering the costs. To evaluate this, the first version uses simple, fixed breakout rules and is compared against a version using conventional fifteen-minute bars. Define the Rules for the First Version The strategy is called “Volume Clock Breakout,” or VCB for short. The initial study uses ETH_USDT.swap and completed one-minute market data bars. Before each new volume bar begins, take the volume from the preceding full twenty-four hours and divide it by 96 to set the target volume for that bar. The number 96 is the number of fifteen-minute intervals in a day. It calibrates the initial scale; it does not mean that exactly 96 bars will form each day. The target stays fixed throughout the bar. Aggregate open, high, low, close, and volume minute by minute, completing a bar the first time the target is reached. Even a minute with extremely high volume produces only one bar. Do not invent an intraminute sequence of prices or reuse excess volume. This method is called “one-minute approximate volume bars.” Volume units must be consistent: coin quantities, contract counts, and traded notional amounts must not be mixed. The trading rules are fixed as follows: Estimate the order quantity as “account equity × risk fraction ÷ (stop price distance + estimated trading cost per unit).” Then apply the maximum notional limit and round down to the quantity step size. If the quantity or margin is insufficient, display the reason rather than increasing the budget automatically. Fix the ATR when the signal is confirmed, set the stop and target from the actual average fill price, and measure the maximum holding time from the first fill. Before trading begins, the twenty-four-hour volume baseline, twenty historical bars, and the data required for ATR must all be ready. Wait if the warm-up is incomplete. The channel must exclude the current bar. The core sequence is shown below; a complete program also needs data, order, and risk handling: let signal = 0; const prior = completedBars.slice(-20); if (prior.length === 20) { const upper = Math.max(...prior.map(b => b.High)); const lower = Math.min(...prior.map(b => b.Low)); signal = closedBar.Close > upper ? 1 : closedBar.Close < lower ? -1 : 0; } completedBars.push(closedBar); Read the historical channel first, then add the current bar. If the current bar is included in the highest-high calculation, a strict upward breakout cannot occur. After confirming a signal, execute using the next available market data. Do not assume a fill at a closing price that has already passed. Checks for a position's stop, profit target, and holding-time limit run independently, without waiting for the next volume bar to complete. Step One: Give the Requirements to the Agent Send this article to the Agent as the requirements specification, followed by these development instructions: Create a new VCB strategy in FMZ JavaScript, supporting ETH_USDT.swap. Implement the volume-bar version according to this article's rules, and provide a fifteen-minute time-bar version for comparison. Both versions must share the signal, position-sizing, and exit code. Use the backtest configuration below for the initial parameters. Check the market data interval, volume units, warm-up length, and trading quantity rules. Process duplicate minutes only once; do not open new positions while a data gap remains unresolved. After a restart, restore data, order, and position state; do not place catch-up orders for past signals. If an order's submission result is uncertain, query the order first rather than submitting it again immediately. Show the breakout channel on the chart. In the status panel, show bar-formation progress, reasons for not trading, orders and positions, account equity, and the strategy's net profit. Complete local tests first, and deliver the source code, parameter descriptions, test results, and usage instructions. After saving to the platform, read the strategy back to verify it, and record the strategy ID and code version. Do not start a running instance yet. For specific API calls, see the GetRecords documentation. The strategy rules and test conditions are provided in this article; the API documentation explains how to make the calls. Local tests should focus on three questions: does the same market data produce the same bars; can the program resume from its previous state after a restart; and can subsequent data rewrite earlier signals? While checking the conditions for opening new positions, continue handling exits for existing positions. Partial fills, duplicate reports, and order submission timeouts need separate local tests. FMZ backtesting uses taker execution with full fills, so it cannot cover partial fills. A simulated intraminute price path does not represent the actual sequence of prices either. See the backtest mode explanation. The Agent has designed the strategy on its own from the requirements: Step Two: Check the Program First, Then Compare the Strategies First, select one week within the development period for a short backtest, and verify the warm-up, bar formation, signals, orders, and profit ledger. If there are no trades, inspect the counts at each stage and use deterministic samples to verify that signals can trigger. Do not relax the actual trading rules just to produce trades. Once the program's flow is working correctly, run the formal comparison. The following fixed configuration is suggested for the first round. All settings are research conditions: Historical period: 2025-10-01 to 2026-10-01, treated as a UTC interval that includes the start and excludes the end. Use the first nine months for development; reserve the three months starting on 2026-07-01 for the final check. Both versions start with 10,000 USDT in simulated capital, a planned risk fraction of 0.25% per trade, and a maximum notional amount of 1,000 USDT. Initially assume, per side, a taker fee of 5 bp and slippage of 2 bp, then add a stress test with both doubled. These are research assumptions; verify the actual fee rates separately. Obtain additional warm-up data from before the start date. If the full history is unavailable, report the available coverage first, then establish a new fixed experiment period. One basis point (1 bp) is one ten-thousandth. Calculate funding fees based on historical positions. If the data is missing, label the results “excluding funding fees”; do not record a missing cost as zero. Both versions start from the same one-minute data, with time bars aggregated on UTC fifteen-minute boundaries. The only deliberately changed experimental condition is the bar construction method; position sizing and exits share the same implementation. Actual ATR values, position sizes, holding times, and trading frequency may change as a result, and the report should list these as well. Run both versions using the fixed configuration and record each backtest ID. Complete the development-period tests and cost stress tests first. Freeze the code and parameters before checking the holdout period. Compare signal counts, actual trade counts, holding times, turnover, gross profit, trading fees, funding fees, net profit, and maximum drawdown. List missing data and execution-model assumptions separately. Do not deduct fees already included by the engine a second time. If the code raises errors, read the logs and fix them, for no more than three rounds. Save each version and retest under the original conditions. Do not continue tuning parameters based on the holdout results, or automatically select whichever period looks best. If gross profit rises while net profit falls, examine the costs of the additional trades. If performance improves during development but fails in the holdout period, examine how dependent the results are on market conditions. If the two versions produce unexpectedly identical bars, or the same signal repeatedly submits orders, return to debugging the implementation first. Successful testing includes correct program behavior and complete records. Whether the strategy has a trading edge is a separate question, judged by its performance after costs. 4. Runtime Inspections: Evidence for Anomalies and Verification for Updates Observe First, Then Verify Orders and Profit After historical testing, start in observation-only mode to confirm that real-time data, bar formation, and signals work correctly. Then use an explicitly designated simulated-trading exchange object to verify order submission and reconciliation. The platform interface uses “live trading instance” as the name for the runtime container. Whether it uses real or simulated funds depends on the connected exchange object. Creating an instance may incur platform fees. The strategy's “Allow order submission” switch does not turn a real exchange into a simulated one either. Before starting, fill in the objects and budget in the following task: Use my designated Docker and simulated-trading exchange object to start the verified VCB version. First report the object IDs, trading environment, parameters, and the results of the funds and order-quantity checks. Operate within the scope explicitly defined for this round; do not modify other instances. After starting, read back the version, data status, orders, positions, and net profit. Record order submission, exchange acknowledgment, actual fills, and cancellation acknowledgment. Do not treat a request as a fill. Keep five categories of information in the status panel: data warm-up, volume progress, signals and blocking reasons, orders and positions, and equity and strategy profit. Keep detailed data in the logs. If there are no trades, trace the issue along this path: One-minute data → Completed bars → Breakout signals → Execution checks → Order submission → Fills If no new bar has formed, the strategy may be waiting for volume. If a bar has formed without a breakout, no signal has appeared. If there is a signal but no order, check quantity, margin, quotes, and orders awaiting confirmation. Count these reasons separately rather than combining them into a single “Conditions not met” message. Account separately for realized profit, unrealized profit, trading fees, and funding fees. Exclude deposits, withdrawals, and profit or loss from other strategies. The status panel can refresh unrealized profit and loss; record profit logs when events occur, such as fills, position changes, or funding-fee entries. Simulated trading first verifies system behavior. A day without a fill does not establish whether a strategy is effective, and a handful of fills does not demonstrate long-term profitability. Make Inspections into Tasks That Actually Run First, manually perform one read-only inspection to confirm that status information and new logs can be retrieved, then set up a schedule: Inspect the designated instance every day at 9:00 a.m. Asia/Singapore time. Verify the running version, parameters, Docker, exchange object, and data status. Read new records from the previous log cursor, and report counts at each stage, reasons for not trading, orders and positions, fees, and net profit. Save the time, evidence, and conclusions to the local project. This inspection is read-only. Do not automatically change parameters, modify code, or restart the instance. Return the schedule record after creating it, and retain a record of an actual run after it executes. If your current assistant does not support scheduling, use an external scheduled task to wake it. Having MCP connected and having a scheduled inspection actually run are two separate things that each need verification. Work Through the Update Process with One Reproducible Problem When an anomaly appears during testing, give the Agent both the raw data and the logs: Reproduce the problem from this inspection record, and identify the code version associated with the evidence. Fix only the identified issue, add regression tests, and retest using the original configuration. Report the changes, test results, and any matters that remain unverified. If the running instance needs updating, first verify how outstanding orders and positions will be handled. Then save the version, update, and restart within the scope explicitly defined for this round. After restarting, read back the startup logs, actual running version, orders and positions, and profit ledger. If no fault has been found yet, you can deliberately test duplicate minutes, missing minutes, or a restart during a local replay to check whether the program handles them as designed. After successfully saving the new source code, you still need to confirm that the running instance is actually using the new version. Retain a code digest, backtest IDs, runtime parameters, logs, and a research conclusion that can be checked, so the next round can build on the existing results. The live trading instance started and supervised by the Agent, with no human intervention, is shown below: The Strategy Used in This Study The source code for the strategy researched autonomously by AI through this complete loop is publicly available

After restarting, read back the startup logs, actual running version, orders and positions, and profit ledger.

If no fault has been found yet, you can deliberately test duplicate minutes, missing minutes, or a restart during a local replay to check whether the program handles them as designed.

After successfully saving the new source code, you still need to confirm that the running instance is actually using the new version. Retain a code digest, backtest IDs, runtime parameters, logs, and a research conclusion that can be checked, so the next round can build on the existing results.

  • The live trading instance started and supervised by the Agent, with no human intervention, is shown below:


The Strategy Used in This Study

items.title: I Had a Full-Time Job, Freelance Clients and Five Side Projects. So I Stopped Before I Burned Out
items.summary: I haven't posted anything for a while, and the reason is not very glamorous: my attention fell apart. I work full-time as a full-stack developer at a fintech company. On top of that, my girlfriend and I have been freelancing for about three years, and together we have completed more than 50 orders. And on top of that , I kept starting side projects. Not finishing them. Starting them. At some point I noticed a pattern. I would open a project, work on it for a few evenings, get an idea for something else and switch. The old project stayed half-done, in a browser tab and somewhere in the back of my head. Every new idea felt like relief. Every old one felt like a small debt. I'm not writing this as someone who "beat burnout". I'm writing it from the middle. I could feel it coming, so I decided to stop before it arrived. What it looked like from the inside There was no dramatic moment. No crash, no breakdown. My week simply had three layers: the main job during the day; freelance work in the evenings; side projects whenever there was "time left", which in practice meant late nights and weekends. The problem was not the amount of work by itself. It was that nothing ever closed. I had five open loops, and each of them asked for attention at the same time. When you switch between five things, you don't do five things. You do five beginnings. Step 1: I took days off from my main job The first thing I did was take a few days off at my main job. It felt strange to step away from the one part of my life that was actually going fine. But that was the point. As long as I was switching between work, clients and side projects every few hours, I couldn't see the whole picture. I needed a few days where I wasn't reacting to anything, just to look at everything from the outside and decide. Step 2: An honest inventory I wrote down every side project and gave each one a single honest status. Not "in progress", because everything is always "in progress". A real status: devtools.abect.com: finished. Free browser-based developer tools: image converters, favicon and meta tag generators, code converters. I started it in April after one too many converter sites full of casino ads. It now lives on its own, and I'm not planning new features. agency.abect.com: almost finished. The site of our small studio. The main part was finished the day before I wrote this; a few fixes are left. abect.com: frozen. A simple website builder. finddax.com: waiting. It finds local businesses without a website on Google Maps. It waits for Abect, because the plan is to connect the two. terraristy.com: being tested. Gaming news and Steam deals. We restructured it recently and are now watching whether it starts bringing search traffic. Writing it down did two things. First, it turned a vague feeling of "I have too much" into a short list. Five lines are scary in your head and surprisingly manageable on paper. Second, it showed the dependencies. Finddax can't really move until Abect does, because the whole idea is that Finddax finds a business and Abect builds its site. That means every evening I spent on Finddax before Abect was ready was an evening spent on the wrong thing. I only saw that once the list was in front of me. Step 3: Pick two. Freeze the rest. Don't kill anything My goal until the end of November is simple: finish the agency site and Terraristy. Everything else waits. Why these two? They are the closest to done. The agency site can also bring paid work, which buys time for everything else. Terraristy has already been restructured, so it mostly needs time and attention, not a rewrite. Why freeze instead of deleting? For me, killing a project feels like a failure, so I keep thinking about it anyway. Freezing is a decision: this project is not dead, it's just not now. It has a place in the queue, and that is enough to stop it from tugging at me every evening. Step 4: Stop doing everything alone This was the biggest change. For a long time I did most of the building myself. That works when you have one project. It doesn't work when you have five plus a job plus clients. So I asked for help: My friend Roman joined to help with development. He built the front end of the new agency site. Dayana Melay designed the new version of the site. My girlfriend is launching ads for the agency site, and together we will look for new development orders. The obvious benefit is less work on my plate. The less obvious one surprised me more: other people create real deadlines. When it's only you, "I'll finish it next week" can repeat forever. When a friend has already built the layout and someone is waiting to launch ads, the project has to move. A small detour about AI The very first version of the agency site was generated by AI. It looked terrible. I use AI tools a lot, and they are great at getting something on the screen fast. But "something on the screen" is not a finished product. The jump from that first version to a site we are not embarrassed to show took a real designer and a real developer. I keep relearning the same lesson: AI speeds up the start, not the finish. Step 5: Make progress visible Before the redesign I saved the starting metrics of the agency site. From now on I'll share what we change and what happens to the numbers, good or bad. The plan for the next one or two work sessions: speed up page loading; add a price calculator widget so a client can estimate the cost of a site on their own; publish two blog posts a week for the next two months. Writing progress down in public is not about looking productive. It's a way to stay honest. A goal that only lives in my head moves every week. A goal I've posted with a date and a baseline is much harder to quietly forget. What helped me, in short This is not a universal method, just what I'm doing right now: Step back for a few days. You can't sort your priorities while you are switching between them every hour. Give every project one honest status. Finished, almost finished, frozen, waiting, testing. No "in progress". Look for dependencies. Some projects can't move until another one does. Work on those first. Pick two and freeze the rest. Frozen is not dead. It just isn't now. Ask for help. Other people bring skills you don't have and deadlines you can't postpone. Make progress visible. Save the baseline, then show what changed. One honest note: I caught this early, while it was still a feeling that burnout was coming. If it's already more than a feeling for you, if you've been dreading opening your laptop for weeks, a list of projects won't fix it. Talk to someone you trust, and consider talking to a professional. What's next At the end of November I'll come back and report whether I actually closed both projects, with the numbers. Until then, I'm curious: how many unfinished side projects do you have right now? Be honest.
items.summary_html:
I haven't posted anything for a while, and the reason is not very glamorous: my attention fell apart.

I work full-time as a full-stack developer at a fintech company. On top of that, my girlfriend and I have been freelancing for about three years, and together we have completed more than 50 orders. And on top of that, I kept starting side projects. Not finishing them. Starting them.

At some point I noticed a pattern. I would open a project, work on it for a few evenings, get an idea for something else and switch. The old project stayed half-done, in a browser tab and somewhere in the back of my head. Every new idea felt like relief. Every old one felt like a small debt.

I'm not writing this as someone who "beat burnout". I'm writing it from the middle. I could feel it coming, so I decided to stop before it arrived.

What it looked like from the inside

There was no dramatic moment. No crash, no breakdown. My week simply had three layers:

  • the main job during the day;
  • freelance work in the evenings;
  • side projects whenever there was "time left", which in practice meant late nights and weekends.

The problem was not the amount of work by itself. It was that nothing ever closed. I had five open loops, and each of them asked for attention at the same time. When you switch between five things, you don't do five things. You do five beginnings.

Step 1: I took days off from my main job

The first thing I did was take a few days off at my main job.

It felt strange to step away from the one part of my life that was actually going fine. But that was the point. As long as I was switching between work, clients and side projects every few hours, I couldn't see the whole picture. I needed a few days where I wasn't reacting to anything, just to look at everything from the outside and decide.

Step 2: An honest inventory

I wrote down every side project and gave each one a single honest status. Not "in progress", because everything is always "in progress". A real status:

  • devtools.abect.com: finished. Free browser-based developer tools: image converters, favicon and meta tag generators, code converters. I started it in April after one too many converter sites full of casino ads. It now lives on its own, and I'm not planning new features.
  • agency.abect.com: almost finished. The site of our small studio. The main part was finished the day before I wrote this; a few fixes are left.
  • abect.com: frozen. A simple website builder.
  • finddax.com: waiting. It finds local businesses without a website on Google Maps. It waits for Abect, because the plan is to connect the two.
  • terraristy.com: being tested. Gaming news and Steam deals. We restructured it recently and are now watching whether it starts bringing search traffic.

Writing it down did two things.

First, it turned a vague feeling of "I have too much" into a short list. Five lines are scary in your head and surprisingly manageable on paper.

Second, it showed the dependencies. Finddax can't really move until Abect does, because the whole idea is that Finddax finds a business and Abect builds its site. That means every evening I spent on Finddax before Abect was ready was an evening spent on the wrong thing. I only saw that once the list was in front of me.

Step 3: Pick two. Freeze the rest. Don't kill anything

My goal until the end of November is simple: finish the agency site and Terraristy. Everything else waits.

Why these two? They are the closest to done. The agency site can also bring paid work, which buys time for everything else. Terraristy has already been restructured, so it mostly needs time and attention, not a rewrite.

Why freeze instead of deleting? For me, killing a project feels like a failure, so I keep thinking about it anyway. Freezing is a decision: this project is not dead, it's just not now. It has a place in the queue, and that is enough to stop it from tugging at me every evening.

Step 4: Stop doing everything alone

This was the biggest change.

For a long time I did most of the building myself. That works when you have one project. It doesn't work when you have five plus a job plus clients.

So I asked for help:

  • My friend Roman joined to help with development. He built the front end of the new agency site.
  • Dayana Melay designed the new version of the site.
  • My girlfriend is launching ads for the agency site, and together we will look for new development orders.

The obvious benefit is less work on my plate. The less obvious one surprised me more: other people create real deadlines. When it's only you, "I'll finish it next week" can repeat forever. When a friend has already built the layout and someone is waiting to launch ads, the project has to move.

A small detour about AI

The very first version of the agency site was generated by AI. It looked terrible.

I use AI tools a lot, and they are great at getting something on the screen fast. But "something on the screen" is not a finished product. The jump from that first version to a site we are not embarrassed to show took a real designer and a real developer. I keep relearning the same lesson: AI speeds up the start, not the finish.

Step 5: Make progress visible

Before the redesign I saved the starting metrics of the agency site. From now on I'll share what we change and what happens to the numbers, good or bad.

The plan for the next one or two work sessions:

  • speed up page loading;
  • add a price calculator widget so a client can estimate the cost of a site on their own;
  • publish two blog posts a week for the next two months.

Writing progress down in public is not about looking productive. It's a way to stay honest. A goal that only lives in my head moves every week. A goal I've posted with a date and a baseline is much harder to quietly forget.

What helped me, in short

This is not a universal method, just what I'm doing right now:

  1. Step back for a few days. You can't sort your priorities while you are switching between them every hour.
  2. Give every project one honest status. Finished, almost finished, frozen, waiting, testing. No "in progress".
  3. Look for dependencies. Some projects can't move until another one does. Work on those first.
  4. Pick two and freeze the rest. Frozen is not dead. It just isn't now.
  5. Ask for help. Other people bring skills you don't have and deadlines you can't postpone.
  6. Make progress visible. Save the baseline, then show what changed.

One honest note: I caught this early, while it was still a feeling that burnout was coming. If it's already more than a feeling for you, if you've been dreading opening your laptop for weeks, a list of projects won't fix it. Talk to someone you trust, and consider talking to a professional.

What's next

At the end of November I'll come back and report whether I actually closed both projects, with the numbers.

Until then, I'm curious: how many unfinished side projects do you have right now? Be honest.
