items.title: Learning the language of machine learning
items.summary: When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work. Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice. Jacob Andreas would rather have the models explain themselves. The newly tenured associate professor develops techniques that enable artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data, in language humans can understand. “Rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate,” says Andreas, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). By studying how machines come to understand language, Andreas and his group work toward building intelligent systems that can learn about the world from human guidance and communicate effectively with human collaborators. They develop methods to make the training process more natural and efficient, so AI models learn in a way that is more like human learning. Ultimately, he and his group want to help people design more accurate and robust deep-learning models that are better suited for their intended application. “We used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. Now, we need ‘mind-reading tools’ that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak,” he says. A love of language Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age. As a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area, he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on. One such book, passed along to him by a family friend, contained a pivotal scene where the main character hacked into a computer system to save the day. That piqued his interest in computers. A few years later, his father brought home a simple BASIC Engine that Andreas could run on their home computer, and he started immersing himself in the world of computer programming. Andreas chose to major in computer science as an undergraduate at Columbia University but wasn’t sure if he wanted to pursue a career as a researcher, as a software engineer, or at a startup. His friends signed up for research projects in faculty labs, so Andreas figured he would try that, too. “I just blast emailed everyone in the computer science department who was working on anything vaguely AI-related, and the natural language processing faculty got back to me first. That is how I wound up in the field where I am now,” he says. Working in the lab of Michael Collins, the Vikram S. Pandit Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, Andreas completed an undergraduate thesis project on machine translation. His project involved adapting existing statistical techniques for representing the meaning of language into more powerful AI systems that could translate passages of text. “I always felt like these deeper questions about how thought works or how to model the world were closer to the surface in language processing problems than in the other tasks that AI people were working on at the time,” he recalls. A seismic shift He wanted to keep exploring deep questions, so Andreas enrolled in graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley to pursue a career as an academic researcher. Before starting his PhD studies, he spent a year earning a master’s degree at Cambridge University in England. In that historic environment, he was inspired to contemplate the nature of language learning as he worked on computational translation problems. Those studies fueled his research when he joined the lab of Berkeley professor of computer science Dan Klein. Andreas began his studies at the time when neural networks were starting to take off. The field of natural language processing was making a seismic shift from statistical methods to this new world of deep learning. Statistical methods utilize transparent, mathematical formulas to analyze text, while deep learning techniques use opaque algorithms to automatically learn complex meanings from massive amounts of text data. “It was fun to be there as we made this transition to the modern toolkit, and learning and inventing all of that stuff when it was still new,” Andreas says. He began collaborating with scientists in computer vision labs to tackle increasingly complex questions about language learning. Together, they designed AI systems that excelled at generating natural language by teaching those systems to “see” and understand the world around them. “This was all super-exciting because there really hadn’t been a common set of tools for working with both language and vision data. Then, all of a sudden, neural networks gave us this common language,” he recalls. He completed a thesis project on the use of neural module networks, which are small fragments of neural networks that perform specific tasks, like localizing objects or logical reasoning, in a larger AI system. But it was the more speculative projects he tackled alongside his thesis, like interpretability and creating natural language descriptions of an AI model’s internal states, that would drive the focus of his group at MIT. Faculty focus After spending a year at the startup Semantic Machines (which spun out of his lab at Berkeley), Andreas joined the MIT faculty in 2019. “It felt like this was a fantastic opportunity to be in the homeland of AI research and collaborate with all these amazing, established people, but also do something new and figure out what the modern era in machine learning was going to look like,” he says. His group focuses on two main areas. First, they are studying the science of large language models to understand the algorithms these models deploy as they learn and process information. The tools they develop help scientists and researchers better predict how a trained model will behave in the real world. For instance, one family of techniques they developed trains large language models to explain what is going on inside other neural networks using language a human could understand. These techniques can assign a natural language description to every information-processing node in a massive neural network. For example, one such description might represent an individual node that identifies “patches of grass near animals” in input images . “That work serves as a jumping off point for a bunch of higher-level questions we ask about how these models represent meaning,” he says. On the other side, his team designs new algorithms for training machine-learning models, and for predicting how specific datasets or examples will affect different aspects of model behavior. “We don’t have a good scientific theory of what is going to happen when you train a model on a particular dataset. This is a big challenge for the field right now,” he says. A changing environment The speed of AI advancement presents one of the biggest challenges his lab faces. The field seems to completely change every three to five years, Andreas says, forcing him to stay nimble and ready to learn something new. That same dilemma carries over into the courses 6.461 and 6.861 (undergraduate and graduate Natural Language Processing), which Andreas co-teaches. He and his fellow instructors must redesign the course each year to keep up with the newest developments. It’s also challenging to teach the technical pieces of machine learning in an era where every assignment could be completed by a large language model rather than a human pupil. “I try to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent,” he says. With so much change, it is difficult to predict where the field is headed next, Andreas says. He foresees that his group’s work on interpretability will become even more important for making advanced systems like AI agents safe enough to deploy in high-stakes situations. This will be especially true as researchers design deep-learning models that can aid in scientific discovery. These models will be trained on troves of raw data from research labs that may not be well-understood by scientists yet. “Figuring out how to enable these models to verbalize all of this hidden knowledge they have about things people have never written about explicitly will be a huge challenge and opportunity for people who work in machine learning,” he says. In addition to tackling challenges in the lab, Andreas enjoys pushing himself as a hiker and backpacker. He has loved spending time in the outdoors since his childhood in California and goes on at least one or two backpacking trips each summer. He and a colleague in the Department of Mathematics are working their way across all the 4,000-foot peaks in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, making slow but steady progress. And now that he has earned tenure, Andreas is looking forward to getting back into an old hobby — singing in a chamber choir. He’s always enjoyed music and became enamored with chapel choirs and bell ringing during his time at Cambridge University.

items.title: He Left Accenture to Build an Embedded SLM—Now It Ranks Among the World’s Best
items.summary: As enterprises adopt AI and move from pilots to production, AI finops is increasingly seeping into deployment decisions. While frontier large language models can write production code and run multi-step agentic workflows, they’re expensive, especially when token costs stack up. Anuj Gupta, Founder and CEO of KiteFishAI, believes many enterprise applications do not require large models. Tasks such as extracting information from documents, classifying customer complaints, and routing support tickets can be handled by smaller, specialised systems . “We wanted to challenge a common assumption in the AI industry that better intelligence always requires larger models,” Gupta tells AIM . The Gurugram-based startup is developing small and large language models, embedding models and enterprise AI technologies. Its work also spans retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), AI agents , scientific AI, and model governance through a product called Prism. From AI Architect to Founder Gupta began experimenting with model development in 2024 while working as a senior AI architect at Accenture, where he spent nearly five years. Access to computing infrastructure, however, became an early obstacle. GPU resources were expensive for an individual developer attempting to build and train models independently. Gupta approached Microsoft for access to Azure computing resources at a lower cost. He used the infrastructure to develop his first model, which he released in January 2026. He later approached the IndiaAI Mission for GPU access and received additional computing support through a government programme. Through the programme, he received ₹50 lakh in government support. He left Accenture in August 2026 to work on the startup full-time. However, the transition also involved personal financial pressure. “I was spending money from my pocket to continue using the GPUs,” he recalls. The startup is currently bootstrapped. That experience has influenced the company's approach to developing AI systems with limited resources. KiteFishAI operates with a small engineering team. For NanoI1, one of its compact language models, the company spent approximately ₹4 lakh on training and development using eight GPUs. Building an Enterprise AI Portfolio KiteFishAI's work extends beyond individual language models. Its areas of development include embedding models , large language models, RAG systems, AI agents, and scientific AI. Embedding models represent text as numerical vectors, allowing applications to retrieve information based on meaning rather than relying only on exact keyword matches. They are used in enterprise search and RAG applications, where AI systems need to retrieve relevant information from internal documents and databases. One of KiteFishAI's models in this category is Nano-Em1-0.6B-v2.1, which the company says ranked ninth globally on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) leaderboard in August 2026. MTEB evaluates embedding models across different text retrieval and representation tasks. The eight-member company is also developing Prism, a model governance product that evaluates model performance across seven parameters through a single API. The product looks to help organisations govern model use and identify potential misuse. However, the startup didn’t share specific details on the seven parameters and enterprise deployments. Liquid AI is another player in the smaller-model space. The company develops Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), a family of AI models designed to be efficient across different computing environments, including edge devices, personal computers, and enterprise infrastructure. The broader strategy is to develop components that can work together in enterprise AI applications. Smaller models can handle classification, extraction and routing, while embedding systems support information retrieval. Larger models can then handle tasks that require more complex reasoning. Although larger systems can handle complex reasoning and a wider range of tasks, they can also require greater computing resources and introduce additional infrastructure and governance considerations. NanoI1 illustrates the company's approach. The 155-million-parameter language model was trained from scratch on approximately 1 trillion tokens using eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. It has a file size of 311 MB and is designed for specialised applications such as KYC document extraction, complaint classification, support-ticket routing, and short-form question answering. The startup claims that NanoI1 scored higher than Google's Gemma-3-270M on HumanEval code generation benchmark, EvalPlus on automated test generation, and grade school math-focused GSM8K. The company has clarified that these results do not make the model universally better than larger systems. Its applications are narrower, focusing on tasks where compact size and deployment flexibility are important. The model is available under the Apache-2.0 licence in Base and Instruct versions. For enterprises, NanoI1 can be deployed on-premises or in a private cloud, allowing inference to take place within infrastructure controlled by the organisation. “A smaller language model is not inherently hallucination-free or secure simply because it has fewer parameters,” he explains. Enterprises still need safeguards such as access controls, encryption, application-level permissions, and human review for sensitive decisions. Moving Towards Multimodal AI Beyond text-based models, KiteFishAI plans to expand into voice, audio, and video. Gupta identifies voice-based models as an area of current focus, with plans to embark on multimodal development over the next two years. India remains its primary focus, and improving language capabilities is part of its development direction. The company also plans to explore longer context windows, specialised models for industry-specific requirements, and integrations with enterprise applications. Gupta expects smaller models to work alongside larger reasoning systems rather than replace them. In an enterprise workflow, a compact model could identify intent, extract information or route a request, while a larger model handles tasks requiring broader reasoning. “See if your task—if it's a particular task that you want—go and use that SLM. Get your task done. Pay less for that particular task,” he advises. items.title: NVIDIA GR00T 2: Human Video Helps Robots Learn, but the Savings Remain Unmeasured
items.summary: Robot time is scarce, and every task taught by remote-control demonstration spends some of it. NVIDIA’s GR00T 2, introduced on November 9, tries to spend less by learning much of its skill from recordings of people at work. NVIDIA’s own tests show that this helps, but they do not yet show how much it saves an operator. What NVIDIA Trained GR00T 2 On NVIDIA unveiled the model at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas. GR00T 2 is a world action model built on NVIDIA Cosmos: one network predicts future video and robot actions together, so it learns how physical interactions unfold along with the actions that produce them. Human video is the largest ingredient by a wide margin. NVIDIA’s research page lists 402,730 hours of egocentric human video in the pretraining mix, against 10,184 hours of handheld-gripper demonstrations and 23,500 hours of robot teleoperation. The footage is annotated, not bare video. According to the whitepaper , it shows proficient workers wearing egocentric cameras, with language descriptions, camera tracking and 3D hand poses attached, and it came from more than 51,500 collectors. NVIDIA has released about 100,000 hours of it on Hugging Face as Human-1M-100K. What the Evidence Supports The cleanest test isolates the human video. NVIDIA pretrained four versions of the model on none, 1%, 10% and all of the human footage, then ran each on 72 tasks with a bimanual robot with two dexterous hands. Real-robot success rose from 18% to 41% between the first and last versions, and NVIDIA says the gain had not leveled off at the largest scale it tested. Each task got three rollout episodes, and a human operator graded each one as a success or a failure. The second result concerns new tasks. On 50 tasks missing from the target robot’s own data, but present in other robots’ teleoperation data, in human video or in both, GR00T 2 averaged 40% success with no fine-tuning and completed 40 of the 50 tasks at least once. One demonstration per task lifted the average to 71%. Five lifted it to 95%, using under three minutes of robot data and a 30-minute fine-tune on a single RTX 5090 GPU. Two further routes cut the robot out more completely. In one, a person wearing cameras, a motion-capture glove and wrist trackers demonstrates a task, and the robot picks up chemistry-lab tasks and a fast conveyor toss with no teleoperated demonstration of the new task. In the other, NVIDIA reconstructs the objects and hand motion from a single human video, trains an expert in simulation and fine-tunes GR00T 2 on simulated rollouts. That policy drove a nail in 9 of 10 real-world trials, while two baseline models, GR00T 1.7 and π0.5, completed none of the real-world tasks in the same test. Where the 95% Figure Needs Context The five-demonstration number is the headline and the weakest guide to what an operator should expect. NVIDIA’s blog post reports the 71% and 95% figures without identifying the tasks. The whitepaper explains that NVIDIA picked the 50 tasks from those the model learns with five episodes at 80% success or better, so the five-episode rate is “high partly by construction.” The 40% zero-shot average covers all 50 tasks and is the broader measure. NVIDIA says most misses come from a single step that falls short on precision within an otherwise correct attempt, and it lists contact-rich skills such as in-hand reorientation and forceful tool use as still hard. The human-only results carry conditions too. The glove demonstrations came from instrumented capture, not ordinary footage. Although no teleoperated demonstration of the new task enters training, the model co-trains on task-agnostic teleoperated play data from the target robot, and NVIDIA reports substantially lower performance from the same post-training data without cross-embodiment pretraining. What Operators Still Can’t Price The implication for operators is that the cost question is open, and NVIDIA’s whitepaper says so itself. It states that it is unknown how much robot performance an hour of each data source yields, that the human-video scaling result shows only that the rate for human video is positive, and that collection budgets cannot be allocated on principle until the rates are measured. It adds that robot learning rarely reports the robot time and human time needed to reach a target reliability. The statistics set a second limit. NVIDIA’s post-training benchmarks use up to 20 trials per task, which the paper says resolves large gaps between GR00T 2 and its baselines but not the differences that matter in deployment. Telling 95% from 99% takes about 285 trials per policy. The partner list points to early-stage use. Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing, Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases, Nexuni is testing it for robotic laundry, and MicroAGI is using it, after reinforcement learning, for Ethernet cable swapping on a YAM robotic arm. NVIDIA’s blog post does not describe any of them as running it in production. Outside testing has to wait. NVIDIA calls GR00T 2 open, but its research page lists code as available in December, and NVIDIA’s Jim Fan told CoRL that the weights for GR00T 2 and a lighter GR00T 2 Turbo, plus the cross-embodiment training recipe, will follow that month, according to Humanoids Daily . At the announcement, NVIDIA had not published license terms for the weights. Every result above comes from NVIDIA’s own tests, including its claim of a top-three ranking on four public benchmarks, which the blog post does not break down by rank or score. What to Watch in December Once the weights and code ship, outside labs can rerun the 50-task evaluation on their own robots and report what a new task costs in robot hours and human hours. That figure will tell operators more than any success rate NVIDIA has published so far. If it comes in low, human video becomes a real answer to the cost of robot data; if it does not, the method stays worth watching.

items.title: Italy Fines Meta €805 Million Over a Facebook Feature That Scanned Android Camera Rolls
items.summary: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante Privacy, has fined Meta €805 million, about $887 million, over a Facebook feature that accessed the photos and videos of Android users without proper permission. It is the largest penalty the Italian regulator has ever issued. The fine targets a Facebook feature called "Get camera roll suggestions when you're browsing Facebook." Available since 2023, it suggests photos and videos from the Android camera roll as ideas for new posts. Why Italy Fined Meta The regulator opened its investigation in July 2025 after a report from the consumer protection organization Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti of Bolzano, and ran its own technical analysis of the app. It concluded that the feature broke Italy's privacy code, which implements the European ePrivacy Directive, and Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code. The regulator found that: Facebook asked for camera roll access with a single, app wide permission the permission came after a vague notice to "enable other features" that did not mention camera roll suggestions the feature was turned on by default around 20 million Italian Android users were affected When granted in full, this kind of permission lets the app read the entire photo library on the device, usually permanently, without the user or the regulator being able to check what is actually used. The Garante says Article 122 protects the smartphone as part of a person's private sphere, so any access to its contents needs free and informed consent, whether or not data is transmitted or harm occurs. Users who have not updated the Facebook app, or who already granted the permission, are still affected. Meta argued that the Irish data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected this, because the ePrivacy rules have no one stop shop mechanism. The case did not cover whether the photos were used to train AI, which Meta denies, and the Garante says it will examine a newer feature from 2026 that processes camera roll content in the cloud separately. The Garante says Meta did not fully cooperate during the investigation, and that this contributed to the size of the fine, along with the number of users affected and a previous 2019 decision against the company. Changes Meta made after the report counted in its favor, but the regulator called them late and limited to users who update the app. The penalty equals roughly 0.47 percent of Meta's global turnover. What Meta Has to Change If Meta does not comply in time, the feature cannot be turned on for users who have not given valid consent. The order requires Meta to: make these changes within 60 days ask for a separate, specific consent for the feature and explain what it does and how to turn it off keep the feature off by default, even for users who already granted the permission report the steps it has started within 30 days and the measures it has taken within 90 days Meta says it will appeal. A company spokesperson called the fine disproportionate and said the feature simply helps people post new content to their Facebook feeds. According to Meta, permission is always required and users can change it at any time in the app's settings. The fine adds to legal pressure on Meta over how it handles user data. In October, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found it had violated the state's consumer protection laws more than 43 million times. Meta has not said whether it will change the camera roll feature in other countries. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: Your AI Spend Has No Owner. Cortex AI Gateway Gives It One.
items.summary: A hands-on production deployment of Snowflake Cortex AI Gateway, covering access governance, live inference, end-to-end tracing, and cost attribution — including the lessons the documentation doesn’t tell you. Most organizations adopted LLMs the way they once adopted SaaS: one team at a time. One group has an OpenAI key in a CI secret. Another runs Claude Code on personal tokens. A third calls Cortex from a notebook. Finance gets one bill and can’t say which team drove it. Security can’t say which prompts left the building. Platform engineering gets told to “govern AI” with no control point to govern from. The friction isn’t the models. It’s that there’s no single path traffic has to take , so identity, logging, and limits have nowhere to attach. On Nov 3, 2026, Snowflake made Cortex AI Gateway generally available: one governed endpoint per account, speaking the OpenAI and Anthropic formats, with every request traced and every credit attributed to a user. I deployed it in a live account and verified every claim here against what came back. The gateway isn’t a new way to call models — it turns AI governance from a policy document into enforced architecture , if you close three gaps the happy path hides. TL;DR Cortex AI Gateway ships open (USAGE to PUBLIC) — revoke it first. Manage the gateway spec as code ; ALTER ... FROM SPECIFICATION replaces it wholesale. PATs need a network policy , or you get a silent 401 with no trace. AI_GATEWAY_USAGE_HISTORY is model-keyed OBJECTs — flatten it for showback. Budgets notify; quotas block. Wire a stored proc for team cutoffs. What you’ll learn: how to lock down the gateway, apply a spec safely, onboard SDK clients (with joined client + gateway traces), query traces and billing, enforce spend, and alert on anomalies — all from a live deployment. Full code: cortex-ai-gateway-starter on GitHub . 1. What changed AI Gateway, Nov 2026: three capabilities GA, two in preview. Three properties shape the architecture: Nothing to provision. One gateway per account, named SNOWFLAKE. Get the endpoint from DESCRIBE AI GATEWAY — private-connectivity accounts use a different host. Open by default. USAGE goes to PUBLIC. Change that first. Path, not entitlement. Gateway USAGE doesn't grant model access; requests still need SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER. That's what makes one chokepoint safe. 2. Before and after Before: many unmanaged paths Before — fragmented access, no attribution After: one governed path After — one boundary, full attribution, full governance Removed: provider keys in secret stores, logging-only LLM proxies, chargeback spreadsheets. Added: a spec managed as code, a sensitive trace table, and one dependency for all AI traffic. (Not to be confused with the Snowflake ML GATEWAY object for traffic splitting.) 3. Production implementation Everything below ships in the companion repo (RBAC, specs, SQL, client configs, CI, runbooks) and was executed in a live account. Step 1: Lock down access (default-deny) USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN; REVOKE USAGE ON AI GATEWAY SNOWFLAKE FROM ROLE PUBLIC; -- it ships open CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS AI_GW_USER; -- may send inference CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS AI_GW_MONITOR; -- reads all usage + traces GRANT USAGE ON AI GATEWAY SNOWFLAKE TO ROLE AI_GW_USER; GRANT MONITOR ON AI GATEWAY SNOWFLAKE TO ROLE AI_GW_MONITOR; -- Model entitlement is separate from the gateway path GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER TO ROLE AI_GW_USER; Verified via SHOW GRANTS: only OWNERSHIP, USAGE→AI_GW_USER, and MONITOR→AI_GW_MONITOR remain. FinOps reads everyone's spend and traces without being able to generate any ; a USAGE-only role sees only its own spans. Step 2: Payload-exclusion tag CREATE TAG GOVERNANCE.TAGS.PAYLOAD_CAPTURE_EXEMPT; ALTER USER EXEC_USER SET TAG GOVERNANCE.TAGS.PAYLOAD_CAPTURE_EXEMPT = 'true'; Only tags set directly on users count, the value is irrelevant, and exclusion fails closed . Anyone who can apply this tag can disable prompt auditing — keep APPLY with security. Step 3: Manage the specification as code ALTER AI GATEWAY ... FROM SPECIFICATION replaces the whole spec — an omitted field reverts to its default. So: spec in Git, apply in full, verify with DESCRIBE. items.summary_html:
A hands-on production deployment of Snowflake Cortex AI Gateway, covering access governance, live inference, end-to-end tracing, and cost attribution — including the lessons the documentation doesn’t tell you.

Most organizations adopted LLMs the way they once adopted SaaS: one team at a time. One group has an OpenAI key in a CI secret. Another runs Claude Code on personal tokens. A third calls Cortex from a notebook. Finance gets one bill and can’t say which team drove it. Security can’t say which prompts left the building. Platform engineering gets told to “govern AI” with no control point to govern from.

The friction isn’t the models. It’s that there’s no single path traffic has to take, so identity, logging, and limits have nowhere to attach.

On Nov 3, 2026, Snowflake made Cortex AI Gateway generally available: one governed endpoint per account, speaking the OpenAI and Anthropic formats, with every request traced and every credit attributed to a user. I deployed it in a live account and verified every claim here against what came back. The gateway isn’t a new way to call models — it turns AI governance from a policy document into enforced architecture, if you close three gaps the happy path hides.

TL;DR
  • Cortex AI Gateway ships open (USAGE to PUBLIC) — revoke it first.
  • Manage the gateway spec as code; ALTER ... FROM SPECIFICATION replaces it wholesale.
  • PATs need a network policy, or you get a silent 401 with no trace.
  • AI_GATEWAY_USAGE_HISTORY is model-keyed OBJECTs — flatten it for showback.
  • Budgets notify; quotas block. Wire a stored proc for team cutoffs.

What you’ll learn: how to lock down the gateway, apply a spec safely, onboard SDK clients (with joined client + gateway traces), query traces and billing, enforce spend, and alert on anomalies — all from a live deployment. Full code: cortex-ai-gateway-starter on GitHub.

1. What changedAI Gateway, Nov 2026: three capabilities GA, two in preview.

Three properties shape the architecture:

  • Nothing to provision. One gateway per account, named SNOWFLAKE. Get the endpoint from DESCRIBE AI GATEWAY — private-connectivity accounts use a different host.
  • Open by default. USAGE goes to PUBLIC. Change that first.
  • Path, not entitlement. Gateway USAGE doesn't grant model access; requests still need SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER. That's what makes one chokepoint safe.
2. Before and after

Before: many unmanaged paths

Before — fragmented access, no attribution

After: one governed path

After — one boundary, full attribution, full governance

Removed: provider keys in secret stores, logging-only LLM proxies, chargeback spreadsheets. Added: a spec managed as code, a sensitive trace table, and one dependency for all AI traffic. (Not to be confused with the Snowflake ML GATEWAY object for traffic splitting.)

3. Production implementation

Everything below ships in the companion repo (RBAC, specs, SQL, client configs, CI, runbooks) and was executed in a live account.

Step 1: Lock down access (default-deny)
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

REVOKE USAGE ON AI GATEWAY SNOWFLAKE FROM ROLE PUBLIC;  -- it ships open
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS AI_GW_USER;     -- may send inference
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS AI_GW_MONITOR;  -- reads all usage + traces
GRANT USAGE   ON AI GATEWAY SNOWFLAKE TO ROLE AI_GW_USER;
GRANT MONITOR ON AI GATEWAY SNOWFLAKE TO ROLE AI_GW_MONITOR;
-- Model entitlement is separate from the gateway path
GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER TO ROLE AI_GW_USER;

Verified via SHOW GRANTS: only OWNERSHIP, USAGE→AI_GW_USER, and MONITOR→AI_GW_MONITOR remain. FinOps reads everyone's spend and traces without being able to generate any; a USAGE-only role sees only its own spans.

Step 2: Payload-exclusion tag
CREATE TAG GOVERNANCE.TAGS.PAYLOAD_CAPTURE_EXEMPT;
ALTER USER EXEC_USER SET TAG GOVERNANCE.TAGS.PAYLOAD_CAPTURE_EXEMPT = 'true';

Only tags set directly on users count, the value is irrelevant, and exclusion fails closed. Anyone who can apply this tag can disable prompt auditing — keep APPLY with security.

Step 3: Manage the specification as code

ALTER AI GATEWAY ... FROM SPECIFICATION replaces the whole spec — an omitted field reverts to its default. So: spec in Git, apply in full, verify with DESCRIBE. I confirmed the round-trip live — what you apply is exactly what DESCRIBE returns:

ALTER AI GATEWAY SNOWFLAKE FROM SPECIFICATION $$
schema_version: 1
models:
  - name: claude-sonnet-4-6
  - name: claude-haiku-4-5
  - name: claude-opus-5
logging:
  enabled: true
  enable_client_telemetry: true
  capture_payload:
    request_response: true
    exclude_tags:
      - GOVERNANCE.TAGS.PAYLOAD_CAPTURE_EXEMPT
$$;

Three deliberate decisions:

  • Allow-list, never '*', in production. '*' exposes every model the account can reach — including ones added tomorrow — with no review.
  • capture_payload.request_response: true is a data-classification decision. It stores full prompts and responses in an event table in your account. Classify it, restrict it, set retention — before enabling.
  • enable_client_telemetry: true lets clients export OTLP spans to /telemetry/v1/traces, joining client-side agent steps to gateway spans under one trace_id (via W3C traceparent).
Step 4: Point clients at the gateway — and the PAT gotcha the docs mention once

The endpoint is https:///api/v2/aigateways/snowflake plus a path per API:

| API                  | Path                    | Models            | SDKs              |
|----------------------|-------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Chat Completions     | `/v1/chat/completions`  | All except Claude | OpenAI Python/JS  |
| Messages             | `/v1/messages`          | Claude only       | Anthropic Python  |
| Responses (preview)  | `/v1/responses`         | OpenAI only       | OpenAI Python/JS  |

Auth is a Snowflake bearer token (OAuth, key-pair JWT, or PAT). Live finding: a PAT works only for a user subject to a network policy. Without one you get a bare HTTP/2 401 with an empty body and no trace. The fix:

CREATE NETWORK POLICY IF NOT EXISTS AI_GW_PAT_NP ALLOWED_IP_LIST = ('');
ALTER USER  SET NETWORK_POLICY = AI_GW_PAT_NP;

And one more syntax catch: PAT creation takes DAYS_TO_EXPIRY, not EXPIRES_IN_DAYS — the latter is rejected.

ALTER USER svc_agent ADD PROGRAMMATIC ACCESS TOKEN ai_gw DAYS_TO_EXPIRY = 1;

Once that was in place, the first real call came back clean:

curl -sS -X POST "$GW/v1/messages" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SNOWFLAKE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \
  -d '{"model":"claude-haiku-4-5","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Reply with exactly: pong 1"}]}'

Response: "pong 1", 15 input tokens, 7 output tokens — plus an x-snowflake-request-id header. Keep that header; it's the join key to your billing record (Step 6).

Step 5: Observability that answers real questions

AGENT_TRACE_TABLE is a table function over a standard event table. The live row for that test call:

| Span                    | Status           | User   | Model             | In/Out Tokens | HTTP | Duration |
|-------------------------|------------------|--------|-------------------|---------------|------|----------|
| `chat claude-haiku-4-5` | `STATUS_CODE_OK` | SATISH | `claude-haiku-4-5`| 15 / 7        | —    | —        |

Token counts match the API response exactly. The production reliability query, verified against the live table:

SELECT
  record_attributes:"gen_ai.request.model"::string        AS model,
  COUNT(*)                                                AS requests,
  COUNT_IF(record:"status":"code"::string = 'STATUS_CODE_ERROR'
           OR TRY_TO_NUMBER(record_attributes:"http.status_code"::string) >= 400)
        / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0)                             AS failure_rate,
  APPROX_PERCENTILE(
    DATEDIFF('millisecond', start_timestamp, timestamp), 0.95) AS p95_ms
FROM TABLE(AGENT_TRACE_TABLE('SNOWFLAKE'))
WHERE timestamp >= DATEADD(hour, -24, SYSDATE())
  AND record_attributes:"gen_ai.operation.name"::string = 'chat'
GROUP BY model
ORDER BY failure_rate DESC;

Two accounting traps and one UI trap:

  • Cache tokens are subsets. input_tokens already includes cache reads/writes — adding them double-counts spend.
  • Payload attributes are opt-in and never populate for exclude-tagged users.
  • Empty Snowsight pages ≠ broken gateway. Before traffic, Overview and Cost show “No usage”. Analytics charts also exclude client OTLP spans and are approximate — alert on SQL, explore in the UI.

For alerting I consolidated to two native alert+procedure pairs (no third-party APM, no scheduled-agent fire, no read-only tradeoff):

  • Hourly AI_GW_WATCHER — spec drift, failure-rate spikes, 429 bursts. Logs every run; emails only on anomaly, naming the failing models inline.
  • Daily AI_GW_DAILY_DIGEST — HTML dashboard email: health pill, KPI cards, 7-day trend chart, per-model latency, top errors, showback. Both headers carry account, region, user, role, and warehouse.
Step 6: Cost management — and the real usage-view schemaSnowsight → AI Gateway → Cost answers the day-to-day questions, filterable by date range and user:
  • Summary cards: gateway spend, median (p50) user spend, model spend, and tool spend (shows “Not available” until MCP tools are in use).
  • Charts: spend trend, spend by model, spend by MCP server, and per-user p50/p90/p99 with a distribution histogram.
  • Tables: model breakdown (credits, credits/request), top 20 users, and a detailed breakdown grouped by model with a period-over-period Δ.

The Snowsight Cost page packages the day-to-day questions (spend cards, trends per model and MCP server, p50/p90/p99 user distribution, top-20 spenders, period deltas). For anything feeding chargeback or audit, the system of record is AI_GATEWAY_USAGE_HISTORY It actually contain:

  • OPERATION_DETAILS and CREDITS_GRANULAR are keyed by model name({"claude-haiku-4-5": {"input_tokens": 15, ...}}) — use LATERAL FLATTEN.
  • USER_ID joins to ACCOUNT_USAGE.USERS; METADATA carries role_id.
  • REQUEST_ID equals the x-snowflake-request-id response header — verified client-to-billing correlation (CREDITS = 0.000025).
One request ID bridges your client logs, trace spans, and billing rows.

The working showback pattern (validated on live rows):

SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('day', h.START_TIME)  AS usage_day,
  u.NAME                           AS user_name,
  f.KEY                            AS model,          -- model name is the object key
  f.VALUE:"input_tokens"::number   AS input_tokens,
  f.VALUE:"output_tokens"::number  AS output_tokens,
  h.REQUEST_ID,
  h.CREDITS
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.AI_GATEWAY_USAGE_HISTORY h
LEFT JOIN SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.USERS u ON u.USER_ID = h.USER_ID
, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => h.OPERATION_DETAILS) f
WHERE h.START_TIME >= DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP());

One subtlety: CREDITS is per-request, so if a request fans out across models (agent turns), it repeats per flattened row — dedupe by REQUEST_ID when summing credits; sum tokens per flattened row.

For enforcement, choose by what actually stops spend:

Three API paths, three SDKs, three model families.

The budget → stored proc → REVOKE cutoff works. I drilled it end to end: the revoke applied, a non-allow-listed role was refused, and the re-grant was logged.

  • Validate the role against an allow-list before any dynamic SQL (IDENTIFIER() inside EXECUTE IMMEDIATE doesn't bind).
  • Quotas are the backstop. Budgets can overshoot for hours; quotas block within minutes.
  • Edition caveat: CREATE BUDGET was unsupported in my account. Budgets and quotas live in Snowsight → AI Gateway → Cost.
Step 7: MCP Tools governance (plan, don’t bet on it yet)

Tools connects agents to GitHub, Slack, Salesforce, Google Workspace and 100+ other systems over MCP, through the same governed path. In Snowsight → MCP & Tools, every server starts disabled — but enabling one without configuring tools exposes all of them.

  • Allowlist specific tools, read-only where possible. “All current and future tools” grows your attack surface with every provider update.
  • Per-user OAuth: the agent can do only what the authorizing user can.
  • Discovery ≠ authorization: clients see servers only with the SNOWFLAKE$OPS.MCP$USER database role.
  • AWS commercial regions only, administered by ACCOUNTADMIN.

Live Demo:

https://medium.com/media/61407ca403e902e8f8869621ae6831c5/href4. Production reality

Beyond the gotchas above, my own deploy skipped a CREATE TABLE — drills catch what reviews don't.

What I learned by deliberately breaking it (a four-case failure drill):

  1. Denied ≠ traced. A request outside the allow-list returns a bare 401 with no span and no billing row — denial happens at the edge. Trace-based failure alerts only see served failures.
  2. max_tokens: 0 succeeds. 200 with stop_reason: max_tokens and zero output — client bugs that zero out output look healthy in reliability metrics.
  3. Malformed requests DO trace. A 400 landed as STATUS_CODE_ERROR with the parse error in record.status.message and, at volume, tripped the watcher's anomaly email.
  4. Failed spans record NULL tokens, and rejections are free. Coalesce the NULLs or they drop out of token sums; the billing view showed only the 2 served requests against 4 trace spans.

Post-drill: p50 323 ms / p95 449 ms for claude-haiku-4-5 through the gateway — the proxy hop is measurable noise at this scale.

What can fail at scale: single-path dependency (add retry/backoff), spec drift (Git + PR + scheduled check), and 429s when a new agent fleet arrives.

Security boundaries: once payload capture is on, the trace table holds customer content, MONITOR reads all of it, and the exclusion tag's APPLY is an audit override.

Migration path: gateway on (metadata-only, explicit models) → one team via snow ai → team by team → revoke old keys → payload capture last.

5. Trade-offsSix dimensions, six benefits, six costs. No net-zero row.
  • Use it when multiple teams or agents call LLMs, finance needs chargeback, or security needs evidence of what was sent.
  • Wait if you need a model Cortex doesn’t serve.
  • Migrate now if either of these is true today:
  • Shared provider API keys live in CI secrets (e.g. an OpenAI key in GitHub Actions). Every call bills to one key, so spend can’t be traced to a person or pipeline, and anyone with repo access can copy it.
  • Engineers run coding agents on personal provider accounts. That traffic has no company logs, no limits, and no record of what code or data left.

Through the gateway, each call carries a Snowflake identity, leaves a trace, and is billed to the user who made it.

6. Architect’s takeaways
  • Revoke PUBLIC USAGE first. The gateway ships open; production is default-deny.
  • Spec as code, applied in full, verified with DESCRIBE. Full-replacement APIs without CI are governance regressions waiting to happen.
  • Path ≠ entitlement ≠ oversight. USAGE, CORTEX_USER, MONITOR — three grants, three owners.
  • PATs need a network policy. Without it you get a silent 401 and zero telemetry — the least documented, most likely first failure.
  • x-snowflake-request-id is your reconciliation key from client response to AI_GATEWAY_USAGE_HISTORY.REQUEST_ID. Log it in your clients.
  • Quotas backstop budgets. Budgets evaluate on a schedule (up to ~6.5h); quotas block in minutes.

The important change isn’t that Snowflake can now proxy LLM calls. It’s that every AI request now carries an identity, leaves a trace, and counts against a budget — verified end to end, from curl to credit — without a sidecar proxy or a spreadsheet.

items.summary:
Understanding prefill, decoding, GPU memory, and inference latency by benchmarking Qwen2.5–0.5B with KV caching enabled and disabled. When we ask a language model to generate text, it doesn’t produce the entire response in one operation. It generates tokens sequentially, using the previously generated tokens as context. But here’s an interesting question: Does an LLM need to recalculate information from all previous tokens every time it generates a new one? Without KV caching, much of that computation is repeated. With KV caching, the model stores previously computed attention keys and values so it can reuse them. I wanted to understand how much difference this actually makes. So I ran a small experiment using Qwen2.5–0.5B-Instruct on a Google Colab Tesla T4 GPU, comparing inference with KV caching enabled and disabled. The initial results were interesting: With a 40-token prompt, KV caching improved generation speed by 1.15× . With a 512-token prompt, the improvement increased to 1.39× . For the longer prompt, caching reduced median inference time from 2.308 seconds to 1.656 seconds. Peak GPU memory allocation increased by approximately 2.63 MB. The experiment highlights an important trade-off: using additional GPU memory can sometimes reduce computation and improve inference speed. Here, we’ll reproduce the experiment step by step using Google Colab, Hugging Face Transformers, PyTorch, and Matplotlib. No model training or fine-tuning is required. What will we build? By the end, we’ll have a notebook that can: Run inference using a pretrained language model. Inspect prefill and token-by-token decoding. Observe how a KV cache grows. Compare generation with KV caching enabled and disabled. Benchmark different input sequence lengths. Measure inference latency and output tokens per second. Analyse GPU memory consumption. Visualise performance and memory trade-offs using Matplotlib. We’ll use the same language model throughout, changing its caching behaviour to understand the difference. Before we begin: What is KV caching? Transformer language models use an attention mechanism to determine how tokens relate to one another. During attention computation, each token is transformed into three representations: Query (Q): What information is the current token looking for? Key (K): What information can this token be matched against? Value (V): What information does the token contribute? ** Think of it like taking notes while reading a long document. Without notes, you repeatedly reread earlier sections to recover important information. With notes, you can reference information you’ve already processed. KV caching follows a similar principle, except the stored information consists of numerical tensors rather than human-readable notes. Setup Google Collab And Run the following to inspect your environment. import sys import torch print("=== ENVIRONMENT CHECK ===") print("Python:", sys.version.split()[0]) print("PyTorch:", torch.__version__) print("CUDA available:", torch.cuda.is_available()) if torch.cuda.is_available(): gpu = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0) print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)) print( "GPU Memory:", round(gpu.total_memory / 1024**3, 2), "GB" ) print("CUDA Version:", torch.version.cuda) My environment looked like this, but it might differ based on available colab Step 2: Install the required libraries %pip install -q \ "transformers==5.23.0" \ "accelerate==1.15.0" \ "huggingface-hub==1.33.0" \ matplotlib import transformers import accelerate import huggingface_hub print("Transformers:", transformers.__version__) print("Accelerate:", accelerate.__version__) print("Hugging Face Hub:", huggingface_hub.__version__) Step 3: Load Qwen2.5–0.5B-Instruct I selected Qwen2.5–0.5B-Instruct . It’s small enough to run on a Tesla T4 and supports standard autoregressive generation with Hugging Face Transformers. import torch from transformers import ( AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM ) MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype=torch.float16 ).to("cuda") model.eval() #Now inspect the model: total_params = sum( p.numel() for p in model.parameters() ) gpu_memory = torch.cuda.memory_allocated() / 1024**3 print("Model:", MODEL_ID) print("Parameters:", f"{total_params:,}") print("Precision:", next(model.parameters()).dtype) print("Device:", next(model.parameters()).device) print("Default KV Cache:", model.config.use_cache) print("Allocated GPU Memory:", round(gpu_memory, 3), "GB") My output: Model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct Parameters: 494,032,768 Precision: torch.float16 Device: cuda:0 Default KV Cache: True Allocated GPU Memory: 0.928 GB Notice the final line: Default KV Cache: True The model is already configured to use caching during generation. We’ll explicitly switch it on and off in our experiments. Step 4: Generate text and measure inference time Before comparing caching strategies, let’s generate some text. We’ll use the following prompt: Explain how solar panels generate electricity in simple terms. First, convert the prompt into tokens using the model’s chat template. messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": ( "Explain how solar panels generate " "electricity in simple terms." ) } ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt" ).to("cuda") Now generate up to 100 tokens while measuring execution time. import time input_tokens = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] torch.cuda.synchronize() start = time.perf_counter() with torch.inference_mode(): outputs = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=100, do_sample=False, use_cache=True, pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id ) torch.cuda.synchronize() elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start generated_tokens = outputs.shape[-1] - input_tokens response = tokenizer.decode( outputs[0][input_tokens:], skip_special_tokens=True ) print("Input tokens:", input_tokens) print("Generated tokens:", generated_tokens) print("Inference time:", round(elapsed, 3), "seconds") print( "Output throughput:", round(generated_tokens / elapsed, 2), "tokens/second" ) print("
MODEL RESPONSE:") print(response) My Output: This first run shouldn’t be treated as a reliable benchmark. It can include initialization and GPU warm-up overhead. The response also stopped before completing its explanation because generation reached the configured token limit. Three terms are important here. Inference latency is the elapsed time needed to produce the response. Output throughput , in this experiment, is the number of generated tokens divided by elapsed time. GPU synchronisation ensures that queued GPU operations finish before we stop the timer. Without synchronisation, Python timing can underestimate GPU execution time because CUDA operations are generally asynchronous. Step 5: Understand prefill and decoding Prefill The model processes the input prompt and calculates the attention representations needed to predict the next token. In our example, the prompt contains 40 tokens. With caching enabled, the model can store the keys and values calculated during this phase. Decode After prefill, the model generates tokens one at a time. When caching is enabled, each subsequent forward pass can process the newest token while reusing the keys and values associated with earlier positions. Let’s inspect this directly. with torch.inference_mode(): prefill = model( **inputs, use_cache=True ) cache = prefill.past_key_values print("=== PREFILL ===") print("Input tokens:", inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]) print("Cache type:", type(cache).__name__) print("Cached positions:", cache.get_seq_length()) next_token = prefill.logits[:, -1, :].argmax( dim=-1, keepdim=True ) print( "
Next predicted token:", repr(tokenizer.decode(next_token[0])) ) decode = model( input_ids=next_token, attention_mask=torch.ones( (1, inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] + 1), dtype=torch.long, device=next_token.device ), past_key_values=cache, use_cache=True ) print("
=== ONE DECODE STEP ===") print( "New input tokens processed:", next_token.shape[-1] ) print( "Cached positions after decode:", decode.past_key_values.get_seq_length() ) My output: === PREFILL === Input tokens: 40 Cache type: DynamicCache Cached positions: 40 Next predicted token: 'Solar' === ONE DECODE STEP === New input tokens processed: 1 Cached positions after decode: 41 This is our first direct observation of KV caching. After processing 40 input tokens, the cache contained 40 positions. We then supplied one additional token, and the cache grew to 41 positions. The model didn’t need to recompute all the previous tokens’ keys and values. An important detail: the cache stores information for tokens that have already been processed, not every token that has merely been predicted. Step 6: Disable KV caching and observe the difference Now let’s disable caching. We’ll perform two manual forward passes. In the first pass, the model processes the original 40-token prompt. In the second pass, we’ll append the predicted token and process the entire 41-token sequence again. original_ids = inputs["input_ids"] original_mask = inputs["attention_mask"] with torch.inference_mode(): first_pass = model( input_ids=original_ids, attention_mask=original_mask, use_cache=False ) first_token = first_pass.logits[:, -1, :].argmax( dim=-1, keepdim=True ) extended_ids = torch.cat( [original_ids, first_token], dim=-1 ) extended_mask = torch.ones_like(extended_ids) second_pass = model( input_ids=extended_ids, attention_mask=extended_mask, use_cache=False ) print("Original prompt tokens:", original_ids.shape[-1]) print("First forward pass tokens:", original_ids.shape[-1]) print("Second forward pass tokens:", extended_ids.shape[-1]) print("Cache returned:", second_pass.past_key_values) My output: Original prompt tokens: 40 First forward pass tokens: 40 Second forward pass tokens: 41 Cache returned: None This demonstrates the computational difference. However, processing 41 tokens instead of one doesn’t mean the second approach will be 41 times slower. GPUs process operations in parallel, and caching introduces its own overhead. To understand the actual speed difference, we need a benchmark. Step 7: Benchmark KV Cache ON versus OFF We’ll use the same model and input prompt, generating 64 tokens for each configuration. We’ll also include warm-up runs and repeated measurements. import time import statistics import torch MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 64 WARMUP_RUNS = 2 MEASURED_RUNS = 3 def benchmark_cache(use_cache): timings = [] token_counts = [] for run in range(WARMUP_RUNS + MEASURED_RUNS): torch.cuda.synchronize() start = time.perf_counter() with torch.inference_mode(): output = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=MAX_NEW_TOKENS, min_new_tokens=MAX_NEW_TOKENS, do_sample=False, use_cache=use_cache, pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id ) torch.cuda.synchronize() elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start generated = ( output.shape[-1] - inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] ) if run >= WARMUP_RUNS: timings.append(elapsed) token_counts.append(generated) return { "median_latency": statistics.median(timings), "median_tokens_per_second": statistics.median( tokens / seconds for tokens, seconds in zip( token_counts, timings ) ), "timings": timings, "generated_tokens": token_counts } cache_on = benchmark_cache(True) cache_off = benchmark_cache(False) print("KV Cache ON:", cache_on) print("KV Cache OFF:", cache_off) speedup = ( cache_off["median_latency"] / cache_on["median_latency"] ) print("Caching speedup:", round(speedup, 2), "x") Note that this first benchmark measures all Cache ON runs before Cache OFF runs. We improve the measurement order in the next step. My results: 40-token prompt Measured speedup: 1.15x Caching was faster, but the improvement was modest. Why? Our prompt contained only 40 tokens, and we generated another 64. The total sequence was relatively short, so recomputing the earlier token representations wasn’t as expensive as it could become with a longer context. This raises the next question: Will the advantage become larger when the prompt contains more tokens? Step 8: Repeat the experiment with a longer prompt We’ll increase the input length from 40 to 512 tokens while keeping generation fixed at 64 tokens. First, create a longer text: paragraph = ( "Machine learning systems process data using mathematical " "models. During inference, a trained model receives input " "tokens and predicts output tokens. Transformer models use " "attention mechanisms to understand relationships between " "tokens in the input sequence. " ) long_text = paragraph * 30 Tokenize the long prompt: long_messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": ( "Summarize the following technical explanation " "in simple terms:

" + long_text ) } ] long_inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( long_messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt" ).to("cuda") long_inputs = { "input_ids": long_inputs["input_ids"][:, :512], "attention_mask": long_inputs["attention_mask"][:, :512] } print("Input tokens:", long_inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]) Our benchmark uses the first 512 tokens for a controlled input length. This truncation can remove the closing chat-template markers, so it’s suitable here for a computational comparison rather than an evaluation of response quality. In an application, we’d truncate the document content while preserving the chat template. Now create a timing function: def timed_generation(use_cache): torch.cuda.synchronize() start = time.perf_counter() with torch.inference_mode(): output = model.generate( **long_inputs, max_new_tokens=64, min_new_tokens=64, do_sample=False, use_cache=use_cache, pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id ) torch.cuda.synchronize() elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start return ( elapsed, output.shape[-1] - long_inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] ) Warm up both configurations: for setting in [True, False]: timed_generation(setting) Then alternate measurement order: results = { True: [], False: [] } for order in [ [True, False], [False, True], [True, False] ]: for setting in order: elapsed, count = timed_generation(setting) assert count == 64 results[setting].append(elapsed) on_median = statistics.median(results[True]) off_median = statistics.median(results[False]) print("Cache ON timings:", results[True]) print("Cache OFF timings:", results[False]) print("Cache ON median:", round(on_median, 3), "s") print("Cache OFF median:", round(off_median, 3), "s") print("Speedup:", round(off_median / on_median, 2), "x") My results: 512-token prompt The benefit increased from 1.15× with the short prompt to 1.39× with the longer prompt. With caching disabled, the model had to repeatedly process a larger history during decoding. With caching enabled, previously calculated attention keys and values were reused. This is consistent with what KV caching is designed to do. However, the benchmark contains only three measured runs per configuration, and GPU timings can fluctuate. These figures describe my Colab environment and shouldn’t be interpreted as universal speedup estimates. Step 8A: Visualise inference latency with Matplotlib Now let’s plot both experiments. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np prompt_lengths = [40, 512] cache_on_latency = [1.695, 1.656] cache_off_latency = [1.950, 2.308] x = np.arange(len(prompt_lengths)) width = 0.34 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5)) bars_on = ax.bar( x - width / 2, cache_on_latency, width, label="KV Cache ON" ) bars_off = ax.bar( x + width / 2, cache_off_latency, width, label="KV Cache OFF" ) for bars in [bars_on, bars_off]: for bar in bars: height = bar.get_height() ax.annotate( f"{height:.3f}s", ( bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, height ), ha="center", va="bottom", xytext=(0, 4), textcoords="offset points" ) ax.set_xticks(x) ax.set_xticklabels([ "40 input tokens", "512 input tokens" ]) ax.set_xlabel("Input prompt length") ax.set_ylabel("Median inference latency (seconds)") ax.set_title("KV Cache ON vs OFF — Qwen2.5-0.5B") ax.legend() ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.2) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() This chart will show that caching improved inference latency in both configurations, with a larger measured benefit for the longer prompt. Step 9: Measure GPU memory consumption So far, caching looks beneficial for speed. But what does it cost? KV caching stores key and value tensors for previously processed tokens, which requires memory. Let’s compare GPU memory allocation with caching enabled and disabled. We’ll measure three things: Baseline memory: Memory allocated before generation. Peak memory: Maximum PyTorch GPU memory allocation during generation. Additional peak memory: The difference between peak allocation and the starting baseline. import gc import statistics import torch def measure_gpu_memory( use_cache, prompt_inputs, max_tokens=64 ): gc.collect() torch.cuda.empty_cache() torch.cuda.synchronize() baseline = torch.cuda.memory_allocated() torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats() with torch.inference_mode(): output = model.generate( **prompt_inputs, max_new_tokens=max_tokens, min_new_tokens=max_tokens, do_sample=False, use_cache=use_cache, pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id ) torch.cuda.synchronize() peak = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() result = { "baseline_mb": baseline / 1024**2, "peak_mb": peak / 1024**2, "additional_peak_mb": ( peak - baseline ) / 1024**2 } del output return result Run three memory measurements for each configuration: memory_results = {} for setting in [False, True]: label = "Cache ON" if setting else "Cache OFF" runs = [ measure_gpu_memory(setting, long_inputs) for _ in range(3) ] memory_results[label] = runs print(f"
{label}") for metric in [ "baseline_mb", "peak_mb", "additional_peak_mb" ]: value = statistics.median( r[metric] for r in runs ) print(metric, round(value, 2), "MB") My measured GPU memory Enabling caching increased the measured peak allocation by approximately 2.63 MB . At the same time, median inference latency fell from 2.308 seconds to 1.656 seconds. This demonstrates an interesting performance trade-off. Is 2.63 MB the KV-cache size? No. This difference represents total peak PyTorch memory allocation between the two execution paths. Both paths use temporary tensors and intermediate computations. The measured difference is not an isolated measurement of the key and value tensors stored by the cache. To determine the exact cache tensor memory, we’d need to inspect the tensors themselves, which is outside the scope of this beginner-friendly experiment. Step 10: Visualise the memory trade-off Finally, let’s create a Matplotlib chart showing the additional peak GPU allocation for both configurations. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import statistics labels = ["KV Cache OFF", "KV Cache ON"] additional_memory = [ statistics.median( r["additional_peak_mb"] for r in memory_results["Cache OFF"] ), statistics.median( r["additional_peak_mb"] for r in memory_results["Cache ON"] ) ] latencies = [2.308, 1.656] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5)) bars = ax.bar( labels, additional_memory, width=0.5 ) for bar, memory, latency in zip( bars, additional_memory, latencies ): ax.annotate( f"{memory:.2f} MB", ( bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, memory ), ha="center", va="bottom", xytext=(0, 6), textcoords="offset points" ) ax.text( bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, memory / 2, f"{latency:.3f}s
inference", ha="center", va="center" ) ax.set_title( "KV Cache: GPU Memory and Inference Latency
" "512 Input Tokens | 64 Output Tokens" ) ax.set_ylabel("Additional Peak GPU Memory (MB)") ax.set_ylim(0, max(additional_memory) * 1.3) ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.2) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() This final chart makes the trade-off visible. In my test configuration, KV caching used slightly more peak GPU memory but reduced inference time. Final results: What did we learn? There are three main lessons. 1. KV caching reduces repeated computation during decoding 2. The benefit depends on sequence length 3. Lower memory usage doesn’t always mean better performance Conclusion KV caching makes LLM inference more efficient by storing and reusing previously computed attention keys and values instead of recalculating them during decoding. In our experiment using Qwen2.5–0.5B-Instruct on a Tesla T4 GPU, KV caching delivered up to 1.39× speedup , reducing inference latency by 28% (652 ms) , with just 2.63 MB of additional peak GPU memory allocation . While 652 milliseconds may seem small, such improvements can add up when processing thousands of requests, although real-world gains depend on the serving workload. The key takeaway: Inference optimization often involves trade-offs. Here, a small increase in memory usage helped reduce computation and improve response time. And with a simple Google Colab experiment, we can measure these trade-offs ourselves. Github Link : https://github.com/arijit1/hugging-face/blob/main/inference/llm_inference_kv_cache.ipynb Does KV Caching Really Speed Up LLM Inference? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Understanding prefill, decoding, GPU memory, and inference latency by benchmarking Qwen2.5–0.5B with KV caching enabled and disabled.

When we ask a language model to generate text, it doesn’t produce the entire response in one operation. It generates tokens sequentially, using the previously generated tokens as context.

But here’s an interesting question:

Does an LLM need to recalculate information from all previous tokens every time it generates a new one?

Without KV caching, much of that computation is repeated. With KV caching, the model stores previously computed attention keys and values so it can reuse them.

I wanted to understand how much difference this actually makes.

So I ran a small experiment using Qwen2.5–0.5B-Instruct on a Google Colab Tesla T4 GPU, comparing inference with KV caching enabled and disabled.

The initial results were interesting:

  • With a 40-token prompt, KV caching improved generation speed by 1.15×.
  • With a 512-token prompt, the improvement increased to 1.39×.
  • For the longer prompt, caching reduced median inference time from 2.308 seconds to 1.656 seconds.
  • Peak GPU memory allocation increased by approximately 2.63 MB.

The experiment highlights an important trade-off: using additional GPU memory can sometimes reduce computation and improve inference speed.

Here, we’ll reproduce the experiment step by step using Google Colab, Hugging Face Transformers, PyTorch, and Matplotlib.

No model training or fine-tuning is required.

What will we build?

By the end, we’ll have a notebook that can:

  1. Run inference using a pretrained language model.
  2. Inspect prefill and token-by-token decoding.
  3. Observe how a KV cache grows.
  4. Compare generation with KV caching enabled and disabled.
  5. Benchmark different input sequence lengths.
  6. Measure inference latency and output tokens per second.
  7. Analyse GPU memory consumption.
  8. Visualise performance and memory trade-offs using Matplotlib.

We’ll use the same language model throughout, changing its caching behaviour to understand the difference.

Before we begin: What is KV caching?

Transformer language models use an attention mechanism to determine how tokens relate to one another.

During attention computation, each token is transformed into three representations:

  • Query (Q): What information is the current token looking for?
  • Key (K): What information can this token be matched against?
  • Value (V): What information does the token contribute?

** Think of it like taking notes while reading a long document. Without notes, you repeatedly reread earlier sections to recover important information. With notes, you can reference information you’ve already processed.

KV caching follows a similar principle, except the stored information consists of numerical tensors rather than human-readable notes.
