        past_key_values=cache,
        use_cache=True
    )

    print("
=== ONE DECODE STEP ===")
    print(
        "New input tokens processed:",
        next_token.shape[-1]
    )
    print(
        "Cached positions after decode:",
        decode.past_key_values.get_seq_length()
    )

My output:

=== PREFILL ===
Input tokens: 40
Cache type: DynamicCache
Cached positions: 40
Next predicted token: 'Solar'
=== ONE DECODE STEP ===
New input tokens processed: 1
Cached positions after decode: 41

This is our first direct observation of KV caching.

After processing 40 input tokens, the cache contained 40 positions.

We then supplied one additional token, and the cache grew to 41 positions.

The model didn’t need to recompute all the previous tokens’ keys and values.

An important detail: the cache stores information for tokens that have already been processed, not every token that has merely been predicted.

Step 6: Disable KV caching and observe the difference

Now let’s disable caching.

We’ll perform two manual forward passes.

In the first pass, the model processes the original 40-token prompt.

In the second pass, we’ll append the predicted token and process the entire 41-token sequence again.

original_ids = inputs["input_ids"]
original_mask = inputs["attention_mask"]

with torch.inference_mode():

    first_pass = model(
        input_ids=original_ids,
        attention_mask=original_mask,
        use_cache=False
    )

    first_token = first_pass.logits[:, -1, :].argmax(
        dim=-1,
        keepdim=True
    )

    extended_ids = torch.cat(
        [original_ids, first_token],
        dim=-1
    )

    extended_mask = torch.ones_like(extended_ids)

    second_pass = model(
        input_ids=extended_ids,
        attention_mask=extended_mask,
        use_cache=False
    )

print("Original prompt tokens:", original_ids.shape[-1])
print("First forward pass tokens:", original_ids.shape[-1])
print("Second forward pass tokens:", extended_ids.shape[-1])
print("Cache returned:", second_pass.past_key_values)

My output:

Original prompt tokens: 40
First forward pass tokens: 40
Second forward pass tokens: 41
Cache returned: None

This demonstrates the computational difference.

However, processing 41 tokens instead of one doesn’t mean the second approach will be 41 times slower.

GPUs process operations in parallel, and caching introduces its own overhead.

To understand the actual speed difference, we need a benchmark.

Step 7: Benchmark KV Cache ON versus OFF

We’ll use the same model and input prompt, generating 64 tokens for each configuration.

We’ll also include warm-up runs and repeated measurements.

import time
import statistics
import torch

MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 64
WARMUP_RUNS = 2
MEASURED_RUNS = 3

def benchmark_cache(use_cache):
    timings = []
    token_counts = []

    for run in range(WARMUP_RUNS + MEASURED_RUNS):

        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        start = time.perf_counter()

        with torch.inference_mode():
            output = model.generate(
                **inputs,
                max_new_tokens=MAX_NEW_TOKENS,
                min_new_tokens=MAX_NEW_TOKENS,
                do_sample=False,
                use_cache=use_cache,
                pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id
            )

        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

        generated = (
            output.shape[-1]
            - inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
        )

        if run >= WARMUP_RUNS:
            timings.append(elapsed)
            token_counts.append(generated)

    return {
        "median_latency": statistics.median(timings),
        "median_tokens_per_second": statistics.median(
            tokens / seconds
            for tokens, seconds in zip(
                token_counts, timings
            )
        ),
        "timings": timings,
        "generated_tokens": token_counts
    }

cache_on = benchmark_cache(True)
cache_off = benchmark_cache(False)

print("KV Cache ON:", cache_on)
print("KV Cache OFF:", cache_off)

speedup = (
    cache_off["median_latency"]
    / cache_on["median_latency"]
)

print("Caching speedup:", round(speedup, 2), "x")

Note that this first benchmark measures all Cache ON runs before Cache OFF runs. We improve the measurement order in the next step.

My results: 40-token prompt

Measured speedup: 1.15x

Caching was faster, but the improvement was modest.

Why?

Our prompt contained only 40 tokens, and we generated another 64.

The total sequence was relatively short, so recomputing the earlier token representations wasn’t as expensive as it could become with a longer context.

This raises the next question:

Will the advantage become larger when the prompt contains more tokens?

Step 8: Repeat the experiment with a longer prompt

We’ll increase the input length from 40 to 512 tokens while keeping generation fixed at 64 tokens.

First, create a longer text:

paragraph = (
    "Machine learning systems process data using mathematical "
    "models. During inference, a trained model receives input "
    "tokens and predicts output tokens. Transformer models use "
    "attention mechanisms to understand relationships between "
    "tokens in the input sequence. "
)
long_text = paragraph * 30

Tokenize the long prompt:

long_messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": (
            "Summarize the following technical explanation "
            "in simple terms:

" + long_text
        )
    }
]
long_inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    long_messages,
    tokenize=True,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt"
).to("cuda")
long_inputs = {
    "input_ids": long_inputs["input_ids"][:, :512],
    "attention_mask": long_inputs["attention_mask"][:, :512]
}
print("Input tokens:", long_inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1])

Our benchmark uses the first 512 tokens for a controlled input length.

This truncation can remove the closing chat-template markers, so it’s suitable here for a computational comparison rather than an evaluation of response quality.

In an application, we’d truncate the document content while preserving the chat template.

Now create a timing function:

def timed_generation(use_cache):
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start = time.perf_counter()

    with torch.inference_mode():
        output = model.generate(
            **long_inputs,
            max_new_tokens=64,
            min_new_tokens=64,
            do_sample=False,
            use_cache=use_cache,
            pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id
        )

    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

    return (
        elapsed,
        output.shape[-1]
        - long_inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
    )

Warm up both configurations:

for setting in [True, False]:
    timed_generation(setting)

Then alternate measurement order:

results = {
    True: [],
    False: []
}

for order in [
    [True, False],
    [False, True],
    [True, False]
]:
    for setting in order:
        elapsed, count = timed_generation(setting)

        assert count == 64
        results[setting].append(elapsed)

on_median = statistics.median(results[True])
off_median = statistics.median(results[False])

print("Cache ON timings:", results[True])
print("Cache OFF timings:", results[False])

print("Cache ON median:", round(on_median, 3), "s")
print("Cache OFF median:", round(off_median, 3), "s")
print("Speedup:", round(off_median / on_median, 2), "x")
My results: 512-token prompt

The benefit increased from 1.15× with the short prompt to 1.39× with the longer prompt.

With caching disabled, the model had to repeatedly process a larger history during decoding.

With caching enabled, previously calculated attention keys and values were reused.

This is consistent with what KV caching is designed to do.

However, the benchmark contains only three measured runs per configuration, and GPU timings can fluctuate. These figures describe my Colab environment and shouldn’t be interpreted as universal speedup estimates.

Step 8A: Visualise inference latency with Matplotlib

Now let’s plot both experiments.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

prompt_lengths = [40, 512]

cache_on_latency = [1.695, 1.656]
cache_off_latency = [1.950, 2.308]

x = np.arange(len(prompt_lengths))
width = 0.34

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

bars_on = ax.bar(
    x - width / 2,
    cache_on_latency,
    width,
    label="KV Cache ON"
)

bars_off = ax.bar(
    x + width / 2,
    cache_off_latency,
    width,
    label="KV Cache OFF"
)

for bars in [bars_on, bars_off]:
    for bar in bars:
        height = bar.get_height()

        ax.annotate(
            f"{height:.3f}s",
            (
                bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
                height
            ),
            ha="center",
            va="bottom",
            xytext=(0, 4),
            textcoords="offset points"
        )

ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels([
    "40 input tokens",
    "512 input tokens"
])

ax.set_xlabel("Input prompt length")
ax.set_ylabel("Median inference latency (seconds)")
ax.set_title("KV Cache ON vs OFF — Qwen2.5-0.5B")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.2)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This chart will show that caching improved inference latency in both configurations, with a larger measured benefit for the longer prompt.

Step 9: Measure GPU memory consumption

So far, caching looks beneficial for speed.

But what does it cost?

KV caching stores key and value tensors for previously processed tokens, which requires memory.

Let’s compare GPU memory allocation with caching enabled and disabled.

We’ll measure three things:

Baseline memory: Memory allocated before generation.

Peak memory: Maximum PyTorch GPU memory allocation during generation.

Additional peak memory: The difference between peak allocation and the starting baseline.

import gc
import statistics
import torch

def measure_gpu_memory(
    use_cache,
    prompt_inputs,
    max_tokens=64
):
    gc.collect()
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    baseline = torch.cuda.memory_allocated()

    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()

    with torch.inference_mode():
        output = model.generate(
            **prompt_inputs,
            max_new_tokens=max_tokens,
            min_new_tokens=max_tokens,
            do_sample=False,
            use_cache=use_cache,
            pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id
        )

    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    peak = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()

    result = {
        "baseline_mb": baseline / 1024**2,
        "peak_mb": peak / 1024**2,
        "additional_peak_mb": (
            peak - baseline
        ) / 1024**2
    }

    del output
    return result

Run three memory measurements for each configuration:

memory_results = {}

for setting in [False, True]:
    label = "Cache ON" if setting else "Cache OFF"

    runs = [
        measure_gpu_memory(setting, long_inputs)
        for _ in range(3)
    ]

    memory_results[label] = runs

    print(f"
{label}")

    for metric in [
        "baseline_mb",
        "peak_mb",
        "additional_peak_mb"
    ]:
        value = statistics.median(
            r[metric] for r in runs
        )

        print(metric, round(value, 2), "MB")
My measured GPU memory

Enabling caching increased the measured peak allocation by approximately 2.63 MB.

At the same time, median inference latency fell from 2.308 seconds to 1.656 seconds.

This demonstrates an interesting performance trade-off.

Is 2.63 MB the KV-cache size?

No.

This difference represents total peak PyTorch memory allocation between the two execution paths.

Both paths use temporary tensors and intermediate computations.

The measured difference is not an isolated measurement of the key and value tensors stored by the cache.

To determine the exact cache tensor memory, we’d need to inspect the tensors themselves, which is outside the scope of this beginner-friendly experiment.

Step 10: Visualise the memory trade-off

Finally, let’s create a Matplotlib chart showing the additional peak GPU allocation for both configurations.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statistics
labels = ["KV Cache OFF", "KV Cache ON"]
additional_memory = [
    statistics.median(
        r["additional_peak_mb"]
        for r in memory_results["Cache OFF"]
    ),
    statistics.median(
        r["additional_peak_mb"]
        for r in memory_results["Cache ON"]
    )
]
latencies = [2.308, 1.656]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
bars = ax.bar(
    labels,
    additional_memory,
    width=0.5
)
for bar, memory, latency in zip(
    bars,
    additional_memory,
    latencies
):
    ax.annotate(
        f"{memory:.2f} MB",
        (
            bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
            memory
        ),
        ha="center",
        va="bottom",
        xytext=(0, 6),
        textcoords="offset points"
    )
    ax.text(
        bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
        memory / 2,
        f"{latency:.3f}s
inference",
        ha="center",
        va="center"
    )
ax.set_title(
    "KV Cache: GPU Memory and Inference Latency
"
    "512 Input Tokens | 64 Output Tokens"
)
ax.set_ylabel("Additional Peak GPU Memory (MB)")
ax.set_ylim(0, max(additional_memory) * 1.3)
ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This final chart makes the trade-off visible.

In my test configuration, KV caching used slightly more peak GPU memory but reduced inference time.

Final results: What did we learn?

There are three main lessons.

1. KV caching reduces repeated computation during decoding

2. The benefit depends on sequence length

3. Lower memory usage doesn’t always mean better performance

Conclusion

KV caching makes LLM inference more efficient by storing and reusing previously computed attention keys and values instead of recalculating them during decoding.

In our experiment using Qwen2.5–0.5B-Instruct on a Tesla T4 GPU, KV caching delivered up to 1.39× speedup, reducing inference latency by 28% (652 ms), with just 2.63 MB of additional peak GPU memory allocation.

While 652 milliseconds may seem small, such improvements can add up when processing thousands of requests, although real-world gains depend on the serving workload.

The key takeaway: Inference optimization often involves trade-offs. Here, a small increase in memory usage helped reduce computation and improve response time.

And with a simple Google Colab experiment, we can measure these trade-offs ourselves.

Github Link : https://github.com/arijit1/hugging-face/blob/main/inference/llm_inference_kv_cache.ipynb

items.title: How to Secure a Shared Lmcache Server on Kubernetes
items.summary: What October’s LMCache CVE teaches about running a KV cache as a shared service, and the setup I’d use In October, a vulnerability in LMCache let anyone who could reach one network port run their own code as root, the admin account that can do anything, inside the cache server’s container. LMCache is an open-source add-on for vLLM, the program many teams use to serve AI models, and most of these setups run on Kubernetes, the system that schedules programs across a fleet of machines. The LMCache team fixed it in 0.5.6, which shipped in mid-October. The lesson is bigger than one bug. LMCache can now run as a separate server of its own, and a separate server needs the same network care as any other shared service. The quick-start Kubernetes example is built to get you running, so hardening it for production is your job. That takes a few configuration changes, a rebuilt image and one coordinated restart. LMCache stores the KV cache, the model’s working memory for a conversation, so the model doesn’t recompute it on every request. That’s what makes long prompts fast, and it’s why LMCache shows up in the vLLM cluster designs I work on. Picture LMCache as a desk drawer. Normally it sits inside the vLLM process and only that process can open it. LMCache’s multiprocess mode, MP mode for short, moves the drawer into its own filing room down the corridor, so several offices can share one set of files. Sharing is the right call, and a shared room needs a lock on the door. RPC authentication is planned for 0.5.7. Until then, the lock is your network setup. LMCache is a separate server now The LMCache docs describe a “DaemonSet + Deployment pattern: one LMCache server per node (DaemonSet) shared by multiple vLLM pods (Deployment).” A DaemonSet runs one copy of a program on every node. A Deployment runs as many copies as you ask for, and each running copy is a pod. vLLM pods connect through LMCacheMPConnector. The cache server holds KV data for every vLLM pod on that GPU node (one machine in the cluster with GPUs) and outlives each of them. A server that runs for months, holds shared state and answers on a network port behaves like Redis, the in-memory database many backends use as a cache. It inherits the security checklist Redis operators have followed for years, and the quick-start example leaves that checklist to you. What the CVE was CVE-2026–105192 scores 9.8 out of 10 on CVSS, the industry’s standard severity score. It affects LMCache 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, plus the 0.5.6 release candidates rc1 to rc3 (pre-release test builds). Only MP mode is affected, because that’s the mode that runs the separate cache server that accepts these messages. Even then the port listens on 127.0.0.1 by default, meaning this machine only. It’s exposed when --host is set to an address other machines can reach, and the project's own Kubernetes example set it to 0.0.0.0, which listens on every network interface. The mechanism is an old one. The cache server decoded one kind of incoming message with Python’s pickle, a format that can carry instructions as well as data. From Python's docs: "It is possible to construct malicious pickle data which will execute arbitrary code during unpickling." The server took those messages over ZeroMQ (a messaging library) on port 5555, with no authentication. One crafted message ran code as the cache server process. In the official images that process runs as root. On an exposed setup, whoever sends that message can run code as root inside the cache server, on a GPU node that is usually among the most expensive you run. The cache holds data derived from every conversation served on that node. The container also sits on the host network and mounts the host’s shared memory, so from there an attacker can reach other workloads’ shared memory and any service listening on the node’s network, not only the cache. Yuval Moravchick of JFrog reported the bug, and it was disclosed on October 7, before a fix existed. LMCache 0.5.6 shipped in mid-October and swapped pickle for versioned, typed MessagePack, which carries only data. It also moved the admin HTTP servers from 0.0.0.0 to 127.0.0.1 and gated POST /run_script, an endpoint that before 0.5.6 was served on every interface with no authentication. Why the quick-start example needs hardening The advisory says to keep the MP transport “on localhost, or on a trusted cluster network only”. A flat pod network isn’t a trusted network, and the shipped example can’t use localhost anyway. Here is the DaemonSet’s YAML configuration file on the v0.5.6 tag, which also moves the port from the default 5555 to 6555: # examples/multi_process/lmcache-daemonset.yaml (abridged) kind: DaemonSet spec: template: spec: hostNetwork: true containers: - image: lmcache/standalone:nightly command: ["/opt/venv/bin/python3", "-m", "lmcache.v1.multiprocess.server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "6555"] # no securityContext at pod or container level # /dev/shm mounted from the host as a hostPath volume hostNetwork: true puts the container directly on the node's own network interfaces instead of Kubernetes' private pod network. The vLLM Deployment finds the cache through the node's address: # examples/multi_process/vllm-deployment.yaml (abridged) env: - name: HOST_IP valueFrom: fieldRef: fieldPath: status.hostIP # kv-transfer-config: "lmcache.mp.host": "tcp://${HOST_IP}", "lmcache.mp.port": 6555 The vLLM pods live on the pod network, so the cache server has to listen on the node’s real interfaces to be reachable. That means every pod in the cluster, and anything else that can route to the node, can reach port 6555 unless a firewall stops it. NetworkPolicy is how Kubernetes firewalls one pod from another, and it won’t help here. Kubernetes leaves its behaviour for hostNetwork pods undefined, and in practice the network plugin treats their traffic as node traffic, so pod selectors never match it. The pod also fails Pod Security Standards, Kubernetes’ built-in security levels, at Baseline. Baseline is the minimum level that blocks the known ways a pod can escalate to the host. It forbids host namespaces like hostNetwork, and it forbids hostPath volumes, which mount a folder straight from the node. This pod does both. The folder is /dev/shm, the shared-memory folder vLLM and the cache use to exchange data on the same machine. The release post plans a localhost-only example for 0.5.7. If you adopt it, check how your vLLM pods reach the cache, because a pod on the pod network can’t reach the node’s own 127.0.0.1. Borrow the Redis checklist From Redis’s security page : “Redis is designed to be accessed by trusted clients inside trusted environments.” Swap in LMCache and the sentence still works. Open Redis instances were hijacked through CONFIG SET, the command that rewrites a running server's settings, and protected mode (plus ACLs later) was part of the answer. Bind address. Redis: docs show binding to 127.0.0.1, and protected mode (since 3.2) answers only loopback when no bind address and no password are configured. LMCache MP 0.5.6: 127.0.0.1 by default, but the example binds 0.0.0.0 on the host network. Do now: never bind a reachable address on the host network. Authentication. Redis: ACLs since Redis 6, legacy requirepass. LMCache MP 0.5.6: no RPC auth in the 0.5.6 release. Do now: restrict who can reach the port. Process user. Redis: “It is recommended to run it as an unprivileged redis user”. LMCache MP 0.5.6: official images run as root. Do now: build a non-root image and set runAsNonRoot. Admin endpoints. Redis: ACL rules plus bind address. LMCache MP 0.5.6: bound to 127.0.0.1 since 0.5.6, and /run_script gated since 0.5.6. Do now: keep them off reachable addresses. LMCache has a second way of passing data, the engine-driven path, that still uses pickle. It’s off by default and can’t be reached over the network, so leave it off. Until RPC authentication and non-root images land, controlling who can reach the port is your main lock. Before 0.5.6, the admin HTTP servers listened on 0.0.0.0, including the MP frontend on port 8080 with its POST /clear-cache endpoint. Run ss -ltnp inside the container to see what yours listens on. Move the cache server onto the pod network If you want one cache server per GPU node shared by several vLLM pods, take it off the host network and give it an ordinary pod IP. NetworkPolicy and Pod Security checks apply to it again. The network change needs no new hardware. It costs engineer time, a rebuilt image and one restart of the cache. Each vLLM pod should talk only to the cache on its own machine. A Service gives a group of pods one stable address, and setting internalTrafficPolicy: Local on it (stable since Kubernetes 1.26) keeps each vLLM pod on its own node's cache server. While that cache server restarts, vLLM pods on the node have nowhere to send cache requests and don't fail over to another node, which is right for a node-local cache. I'd keep it that way. Confirm that kube-proxy, the component that routes Service traffic on each node, honors the field in your cluster. With the policy below, only pods labelled vllm can connect. Traffic from the pod's own node is still allowed, which is how kubelet health probes get through, so a compromised process on that node bypasses the policy. You also clear the hostNetwork violation. The pod still fails Baseline while it mounts /dev/shm as a hostPath volume. The deployment guide documents --isolated-ipc (MP connector only, needs cuda-python), which drops the shared-folder dependency for IPC, inter-process communication between vLLM and the cache. That's the route to Baseline and then to Restricted, the strictest level. If you don’t need sharing across pods, run one cache server inside each vLLM pod over localhost. You lose the shared cache, and there’s no port the rest of the cluster can reach. A second container would need the same GPU visible and a shared memory volume for IPC. The manifests below are the target setup. Take them through staging before production and confirm: data still passes between vLLM and the cache after the user change, vLLM keeps serving while a node’s cache server restarts, and vLLM fails cleanly, with a clear connector error, when the cache server rejects its version. apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: lmcache namespace: inference spec: selector: app: lmcache internalTrafficPolicy: Local ports: - name: zmq port: 5555 targetPort: 5555 --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: default-deny-ingress namespace: inference spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: ["Ingress"] --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: lmcache-from-vllm-only namespace: inference spec: podSelector: matchLabels: app: lmcache policyTypes: ["Ingress"] ingress: - from: - podSelector: matchLabels: app: vllm ports: - protocol: TCP port: 5555 These settings run the cache as an ordinary user with no extra Linux privileges, so a break-in lands with far less power than root. spec: hostNetwork: false securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 10001 seccompProfile: type: RuntimeDefault containers: - name: lmcache image: your-registry/lmcache-standalone:0.5.6-nonroot # built from the Dockerfile; never :nightly command: ["/opt/venv/bin/python3", "-m", "lmcache.v1.multiprocess.server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "5555"] # 0.0.0.0 here is the pod IP securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] Then point vLLM at tcp://lmcache.inference.svc.cluster.local on port 5555 instead of ${HOST_IP}. Without an allow rule, the default-deny policy cuts off your gateway too. Add one for vLLM’s serving port (8000 by default) from your gateway or ingress namespace, and one for your Prometheus namespace if you scrape LMCache metrics on 9090 as the deployment guide does. The labels have to match. The manifests above use app: lmcache and app: vllm in namespace inference, so set the labels and namespace to match your own deployment. A Service whose selector matches nothing fails silently. HTTP health checks break. The guide’s HTTP variant has the kubelet (the agent on each node that starts pods and checks their health) probe /healthcheck on 8080, which fails now that 0.5.6 binds HTTP to 127.0.0.1. Use an exec probe that checks the process from inside the container. Don’t mix versions. A 0.5.5 component can’t talk to a 0.5.6 one, because the wire format changed. The user change needs care too. In legacy IPC mode vLLM and the cache server share /dev/shm, so they have to run as the same UID, the numeric user ID a process runs under. That means runAsUser: 10001 on the vLLM pod too, with its model and cache directories on writable paths. It isn't needed if you use --isolated-ipc. Mount an emptyDir (a scratch folder Kubernetes creates for the pod and deletes with it) for any path the image writes to, such as temp or cache directories. Check that NetworkPolicy is enforced A NetworkPolicy nobody enforces looks identical to one that works, because the API server accepts the YAML either way. From the Kubernetes docs : “Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.” Enforcement comes from the CNI, the network plugin that moves packets between pods. Calico and Cilium enforce it. Flannel alone doesn’t (its README says flanneld “does not natively enforce Network Policies”), so pair it with Calico or Cilium. On EKS with the AWS VPC CNI, enforcement is off until you set enableNetworkPolicy in the add-on's configuration. AWS also notes that its strict mode doesn't apply default deny to host-networked pods. Stand up a labeled node pool with the 0.5.6 DaemonSet and a matching vLLM Deployment pinned to it, shift traffic at the load balancer, then drain the old pool (stop sending it new traffic and let in-flight requests finish). Scale vLLM to zero, roll the DaemonSet, bring vLLM back, and users lose the service for that window. Either way the warm cache in the cache server’s memory is gone, because the cache server restarts. Until the cache warms up again, repeated long prompts are recomputed from scratch and respond as slowly as if there were no cache. Schedule the cutover for your quietest hour. I compared these strategies in an earlier post, Stop Defaulting to Rolling Updates: 6 Kubernetes Deployment Strategies Explained . The 0.5.6 release post plans RPC authentication and a localhost-bound example for 0.5.7, and points to 0.5.7 for non-root images. Until then, assume the cache port (5555 by default, 6555 in the shipped example) is reachable by anything you haven’t blocked. If you run LMCache MP mode on Kubernetes, which setup did you land on: host network, pod network, or a cache server inside each vLLM pod? I’d like to compare notes. If this resonated and you want to go deeper on the technical side, the architecture decisions, the infra tradeoffs and the detail that doesn’t fit in a blog post, connect with me on LinkedIn . items.summary_html:
What October’s LMCache CVE teaches about running a KV cache as a shared service, and the setup I’d use

In October, a vulnerability in LMCache let anyone who could reach one network port run their own code as root, the admin account that can do anything, inside the cache server’s container. LMCache is an open-source add-on for vLLM, the program many teams use to serve AI models, and most of these setups run on Kubernetes, the system that schedules programs across a fleet of machines.

The LMCache team fixed it in 0.5.6, which shipped in mid-October. The lesson is bigger than one bug. LMCache can now run as a separate server of its own, and a separate server needs the same network care as any other shared service. The quick-start Kubernetes example is built to get you running, so hardening it for production is your job. That takes a few configuration changes, a rebuilt image and one coordinated restart.

LMCache stores the KV cache, the model’s working memory for a conversation, so the model doesn’t recompute it on every request. That’s what makes long prompts fast, and it’s why LMCache shows up in the vLLM cluster designs I work on.

Picture LMCache as a desk drawer. Normally it sits inside the vLLM process and only that process can open it. LMCache’s multiprocess mode, MP mode for short, moves the drawer into its own filing room down the corridor, so several offices can share one set of files. Sharing is the right call, and a shared room needs a lock on the door. RPC authentication is planned for 0.5.7. Until then, the lock is your network setup.

LMCache is a separate server now

The LMCache docs describe a “DaemonSet + Deployment pattern: one LMCache server per node (DaemonSet) shared by multiple vLLM pods (Deployment).” A DaemonSet runs one copy of a program on every node. A Deployment runs as many copies as you ask for, and each running copy is a pod. vLLM pods connect through LMCacheMPConnector. The cache server holds KV data for every vLLM pod on that GPU node (one machine in the cluster with GPUs) and outlives each of them.

A server that runs for months, holds shared state and answers on a network port behaves like Redis, the in-memory database many backends use as a cache. It inherits the security checklist Redis operators have followed for years, and the quick-start example leaves that checklist to you.

What the CVE was

CVE-2026–105192 scores 9.8 out of 10 on CVSS, the industry’s standard severity score. It affects LMCache 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, plus the 0.5.6 release candidates rc1 to rc3 (pre-release test builds). Only MP mode is affected, because that’s the mode that runs the separate cache server that accepts these messages. Even then the port listens on 127.0.0.1 by default, meaning this machine only. It’s exposed when --host is set to an address other machines can reach, and the project's own Kubernetes example set it to 0.0.0.0, which listens on every network interface.

The mechanism is an old one. The cache server decoded one kind of incoming message with Python’s pickle, a format that can carry instructions as well as data. From Python's docs: "It is possible to construct malicious pickle data which will execute arbitrary code during unpickling." The server took those messages over ZeroMQ (a messaging library) on port 5555, with no authentication. One crafted message ran code as the cache server process. In the official images that process runs as root.

On an exposed setup, whoever sends that message can run code as root inside the cache server, on a GPU node that is usually among the most expensive you run. The cache holds data derived from every conversation served on that node. The container also sits on the host network and mounts the host’s shared memory, so from there an attacker can reach other workloads’ shared memory and any service listening on the node’s network, not only the cache.

Yuval Moravchick of JFrog reported the bug, and it was disclosed on October 7, before a fix existed. LMCache 0.5.6 shipped in mid-October and swapped pickle for versioned, typed MessagePack, which carries only data. It also moved the admin HTTP servers from 0.0.0.0 to 127.0.0.1 and gated POST /run_script, an endpoint that before 0.5.6 was served on every interface with no authentication.

Why the quick-start example needs hardening

The advisory says to keep the MP transport “on localhost, or on a trusted cluster network only”. A flat pod network isn’t a trusted network, and the shipped example can’t use localhost anyway. Here is the DaemonSet’s YAML configuration file on the v0.5.6 tag, which also moves the port from the default 5555 to 6555:

# examples/multi_process/lmcache-daemonset.yaml (abridged)
kind: DaemonSet
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      hostNetwork: true
      containers:
      - image: lmcache/standalone:nightly
        command: ["/opt/venv/bin/python3", "-m", "lmcache.v1.multiprocess.server",
                  "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "6555"]
        # no securityContext at pod or container level
        # /dev/shm mounted from the host as a hostPath volume

hostNetwork: true puts the container directly on the node's own network interfaces instead of Kubernetes' private pod network. The vLLM Deployment finds the cache through the node's address:

# examples/multi_process/vllm-deployment.yaml (abridged)
env:
- name: HOST_IP
  valueFrom:
    fieldRef:
      fieldPath: status.hostIP
# kv-transfer-config: "lmcache.mp.host": "tcp://${HOST_IP}", "lmcache.mp.port": 6555

The vLLM pods live on the pod network, so the cache server has to listen on the node’s real interfaces to be reachable. That means every pod in the cluster, and anything else that can route to the node, can reach port 6555 unless a firewall stops it.

NetworkPolicy is how Kubernetes firewalls one pod from another, and it won’t help here. Kubernetes leaves its behaviour for hostNetwork pods undefined, and in practice the network plugin treats their traffic as node traffic, so pod selectors never match it.

The pod also fails Pod Security Standards, Kubernetes’ built-in security levels, at Baseline. Baseline is the minimum level that blocks the known ways a pod can escalate to the host. It forbids host namespaces like hostNetwork, and it forbids hostPath volumes, which mount a folder straight from the node. This pod does both. The folder is /dev/shm, the shared-memory folder vLLM and the cache use to exchange data on the same machine.

The release post plans a localhost-only example for 0.5.7. If you adopt it, check how your vLLM pods reach the cache, because a pod on the pod network can’t reach the node’s own 127.0.0.1.

Borrow the Redis checklist

From Redis’s security page: “Redis is designed to be accessed by trusted clients inside trusted environments.” Swap in LMCache and the sentence still works. Open Redis instances were hijacked through CONFIG SET, the command that rewrites a running server's settings, and protected mode (plus ACLs later) was part of the answer.

  • Bind address. Redis: docs show binding to 127.0.0.1, and protected mode (since 3.2) answers only loopback when no bind address and no password are configured. LMCache MP 0.5.6: 127.0.0.1 by default, but the example binds 0.0.0.0 on the host network. Do now: never bind a reachable address on the host network.
  • Authentication. Redis: ACLs since Redis 6, legacy requirepass. LMCache MP 0.5.6: no RPC auth in the 0.5.6 release. Do now: restrict who can reach the port.
  • Process user. Redis: “It is recommended to run it as an unprivileged redis user”. LMCache MP 0.5.6: official images run as root. Do now: build a non-root image and set runAsNonRoot.
  • Admin endpoints. Redis: ACL rules plus bind address. LMCache MP 0.5.6: bound to 127.0.0.1 since 0.5.6, and /run_script gated since 0.5.6. Do now: keep them off reachable addresses.

LMCache has a second way of passing data, the engine-driven path, that still uses pickle. It’s off by default and can’t be reached over the network, so leave it off.

Until RPC authentication and non-root images land, controlling who can reach the port is your main lock.

Before 0.5.6, the admin HTTP servers listened on 0.0.0.0, including the MP frontend on port 8080 with its POST /clear-cache endpoint. Run ss -ltnp inside the container to see what yours listens on.

Move the cache server onto the pod network

If you want one cache server per GPU node shared by several vLLM pods, take it off the host network and give it an ordinary pod IP. NetworkPolicy and Pod Security checks apply to it again. The network change needs no new hardware. It costs engineer time, a rebuilt image and one restart of the cache.

Each vLLM pod should talk only to the cache on its own machine. A Service gives a group of pods one stable address, and setting internalTrafficPolicy: Local on it (stable since Kubernetes 1.26) keeps each vLLM pod on its own node's cache server. While that cache server restarts, vLLM pods on the node have nowhere to send cache requests and don't fail over to another node, which is right for a node-local cache. I'd keep it that way. Confirm that kube-proxy, the component that routes Service traffic on each node, honors the field in your cluster.

With the policy below, only pods labelled vllm can connect. Traffic from the pod's own node is still allowed, which is how kubelet health probes get through, so a compromised process on that node bypasses the policy.

You also clear the hostNetwork violation. The pod still fails Baseline while it mounts /dev/shm as a hostPath volume. The deployment guide documents --isolated-ipc (MP connector only, needs cuda-python), which drops the shared-folder dependency for IPC, inter-process communication between vLLM and the cache. That's the route to Baseline and then to Restricted, the strictest level.

If you don’t need sharing across pods, run one cache server inside each vLLM pod over localhost. You lose the shared cache, and there’s no port the rest of the cluster can reach. A second container would need the same GPU visible and a shared memory volume for IPC.

The manifests below are the target setup. Take them through staging before production and confirm: data still passes between vLLM and the cache after the user change, vLLM keeps serving while a node’s cache server restarts, and vLLM fails cleanly, with a clear connector error, when the cache server rejects its version.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: lmcache
  namespace: inference
spec:
  selector:
    app: lmcache
  internalTrafficPolicy: Local
  ports:
  - name: zmq
    port: 5555
    targetPort: 5555
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: inference
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: lmcache-from-vllm-only
  namespace: inference
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: lmcache
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: vllm
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5555

These settings run the cache as an ordinary user with no extra Linux privileges, so a break-in lands with far less power than root.

spec:
  hostNetwork: false
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: lmcache
    image: your-registry/lmcache-standalone:0.5.6-nonroot   # built from the Dockerfile; never :nightly
    command: ["/opt/venv/bin/python3", "-m", "lmcache.v1.multiprocess.server",
              "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "5555"]   # 0.0.0.0 here is the pod IP
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]

Then point vLLM at tcp://lmcache.inference.svc.cluster.local on port 5555 instead of ${HOST_IP}.

  • Without an allow rule, the default-deny policy cuts off your gateway too. Add one for vLLM’s serving port (8000 by default) from your gateway or ingress namespace, and one for your Prometheus namespace if you scrape LMCache metrics on 9090 as the deployment guide does.
  • The labels have to match. The manifests above use app: lmcache and app: vllm in namespace inference, so set the labels and namespace to match your own deployment. A Service whose selector matches nothing fails silently.
  • HTTP health checks break. The guide’s HTTP variant has the kubelet (the agent on each node that starts pods and checks their health) probe /healthcheck on 8080, which fails now that 0.5.6 binds HTTP to 127.0.0.1. Use an exec probe that checks the process from inside the container.
  • Don’t mix versions. A 0.5.5 component can’t talk to a 0.5.6 one, because the wire format changed.

The user change needs care too. In legacy IPC mode vLLM and the cache server share /dev/shm, so they have to run as the same UID, the numeric user ID a process runs under.

That means runAsUser: 10001 on the vLLM pod too, with its model and cache directories on writable paths. It isn't needed if you use --isolated-ipc. Mount an emptyDir (a scratch folder Kubernetes creates for the pod and deletes with it) for any path the image writes to, such as temp or cache directories.

Check that NetworkPolicy is enforced

A NetworkPolicy nobody enforces looks identical to one that works, because the API server accepts the YAML either way. From the Kubernetes docs: “Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.” Enforcement comes from the CNI, the network plugin that moves packets between pods.

Calico and Cilium enforce it. Flannel alone doesn’t (its README says flanneld “does not natively enforce Network Policies”), so pair it with Calico or Cilium. On EKS with the AWS VPC CNI, enforcement is off until you set enableNetworkPolicy in the add-on's configuration. AWS also notes that its strict mode doesn't apply default deny to host-networked pods.

If you manage the team, ask whether your cluster enforces NetworkPolicy and how that was checked.

To check, schedule a throwaway pod without the app: vllm label onto a node that runs a cache server (set nodeName) and connect straight to the cache server's pod IP on 5555. Don't test through the Service alone. With internalTrafficPolicy: Local, a pod on a node without a cache server fails to connect whether or not policy works.

If you have to keep the host network, you need a firewall on the node itself, because pod-level rules don’t see this traffic. Where your CNI gives each node its own pod CIDR (the address range Kubernetes hands to pods on that node), a host firewall rule can accept 6555 only from that range. Check the source IP the node actually sees, because address translation in overlay networks can hide the pod range. The AWS VPC CNI has no per-node pod CIDR, so use security groups for pods or rules that match the local pod interfaces. Calico host endpoint policies and Cilium host policies can be scoped the same way.

Upgrade both sides at once

From the 0.5.6 release post: “0.5.6 cannot communicate with earlier versions.” The wire format, the exact layout of the messages the two sides exchange, changed. Every vLLM pod and every cache server has to move together.

A DaemonSet rolling update doesn’t do that. It replaces cache servers node by node while your vLLM Deployment rolls on its own schedule. The vLLM side’s version is the lmcache package inside your vLLM image, and the example uses lmcache/vllm-openai:latest-nightly, so with nightly tags you can end up with mixed versions without planning any upgrade. Find out in staging what your vLLM version does when the cache server rejects it.

A plain kubectl apply gives you that red zone. Blue-green by node pool avoids it by running old and new side by side and switching traffic in one move. Stand up a labeled node pool with the 0.5.6 DaemonSet and a matching vLLM Deployment pinned to it, shift traffic at the load balancer, then drain the old pool (stop sending it new traffic and let in-flight requests finish). You pay for a second set of GPUs during the overlap, so keep the window short.

If you can take downtime, recreate is simpler. Scale vLLM to zero, roll the DaemonSet, bring vLLM back, and users lose the service for that window.

Either way the warm cache in the cache server’s memory is gone, because the cache server restarts. Until the cache warms up again, repeated long prompts are recomputed from scratch and respond as slowly as if there were no cache. Schedule the cutover for your quietest hour. I compared these strategies in an earlier post, Stop Defaulting to Rolling Updates: 6 Kubernetes Deployment Strategies Explained. For this upgrade, pick blue-green if you can’t take downtime and recreate if you can. Never a plain rolling update.

Pin image tags on both sides, watch the vLLM logs for connector errors during cutover, treat any release note that mentions the wire format as a migration, and name one owner for the cutover.

What’s planned for 0.5.7

The LMCache team has already said what comes next. The 0.5.6 release post plans RPC authentication and a localhost-bound example for 0.5.7, and points to 0.5.7 for non-root images. As of November 11, 0.5.6 is the latest stable release, so re-check all three when 0.5.7 lands. Until then, assume the cache port (5555 by default, 6555 in the shipped example) is reachable by anything you haven’t blocked.

If you run LMCache MP mode on Kubernetes, which setup did you land on: host network, pod network, or a cache server inside each vLLM pod? I’d like to compare notes.

If this resonated and you want to go deeper on the technical side, the architecture decisions, the infra tradeoffs and the detail that doesn’t fit in a blog post, connect with me on LinkedIn. I’m always up for a good conversation about the unglamorous reality of building AI systems that actually work.

items.title: From 200 Users to a Bill of Materials for a Private Llm Server
items.summary: How many users a GPU server really serves, and why memory alone gives the wrong answer Almost every private LLM request I get in presales opens with “which GPU should we buy?” I start somewhere duller. How many people will use it at once, how much text will they paste in, and how long will they wait for a reply? Take a company that wants its own AI assistant for 200 employees, running on its own hardware instead of a cloud API. Answer those questions and you land on one server with four GPUs, the chips that do the model’s math. That server has enough memory for well over 100 conversations, but I size it to handle only 30 to 50 at once. An LLM server is a restaurant kitchen The GPU is the kitchen. Its memory is the counter space. The chef’s recipe book stays on that counter all the time. That’s the model’s weights , the numbers it learned during training. Each diner who is still eating has an order ticket pinned there too, and the ticket gets longer as the conversation goes on. In LLM terms, that ticket is the KV cache . It holds the model’s notes on everything already said in the conversation, so it doesn’t have to re-read the whole chat for every new word. While the ticket stays pinned up, the conversation is warm . Clear it, and the chef has to read the whole order again from the top. Throughput is how fast the kitchen cooks, measured in tokens per second. A token is about three-quarters of a word. Reading the order before cooking is called prefill , and a long order takes a while to read. What “200 users” really means Everything below comes from four numbers. If you can get only one of them from your logs, get the first. People getting an answer at the same moment. Value for this example: 30 (15% of 200). Why it matters: How busy the kitchen is. Typical request length. Value for this example: 8K tokens, about 6,000 words. Why it matters: Ticket size and reading time. Worst case. Value for this example: 32K tokens, someone pastes a contract. Why it matters: The request that breaks your sizing. What “served” means. Value for this example: First word within 2 s (engineers call it TTFT, time to first token), then at least 20 tokens/s. Why it matters: Smooth streaming, several times faster than most people read. 15% is generous for an internal assistant. Your chat logs, or the API gateway that sits in front of the model, will show you the real peak. The model is Llama 3.3 70B. It’s a big open model, its specs are public, and NVIDIA has benchmarked it on the exact card I’m sizing.I work top to bottom in that funnel, and the GPU doesn’t show up until the last row. The size of one conversation in memory For every token the model has seen, it keeps a small record in GPU memory, one per layer. A layer is one of the model’s stacked processing steps. How big that record is depends on precision, the number of bits each stored number gets. Fewer bits make a smaller ticket and a slightly less exact one. There are three common choices: BF16 at 16 bits, FP8 at 8 bits, and NVFP4 at 4 bits plus a little bookkeeping. KV bytes per token = 2 (keys and values) x layers x KV heads x head_dim x bytes per number Llama 3.3 70B’s spec file , config.json, is public and lists 80 layers, 8 KV heads and a head dimension of 128. The last two set how wide each record is. At 16 bits per number (BF16), each token costs 327,680 bytes, or 320 KiB, about a third of a megabyte. FP8 halves that to 160 KiB, and NVFP4 brings it down to about 94 KiB in practice, because of the bookkeeping bits. So one 8K-token conversation is a 2.7 GB ticket at BF16 and 1.3 GB at FP8. Thirty people at 8K each puts about 245,000 tokens in memory at once, roughly 40 GB of counter space at FP8. At 32K, those thirty conversations need about 160 GB. That’s almost the entire cache budget of the server I end up with, eaten by thirty people pasting contracts. Four cards, four copies The GPU here is the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. It has 96 GB of memory, so four of them give you 384 GB of counter space. It reads that memory at about 1.6 TB/s, and that speed mostly decides how fast it writes each new word. You can cap its power anywhere between 400 W and 600 W. These cards have no NVLink, NVIDIA’s fast private link between GPUs. They talk to each other over PCIe, the ordinary connection between the CPU and everything plugged into the motherboard, and PCIe is far slower. You could split one copy of the model across all four cards. That’s called tensor parallelism, and it keeps the cards swapping data over that slow link all the time. I’d rather run four separate copies, one per card, and put a load balancer in front to decide which copy answers which person. Each copy is called a replica. That only works if the model fits on one card. Llama 3.3 70B has 70.6 billion weights. Squeeze each one down to about 4.5 bits, which is called quantization (here using NVFP4), and the whole model comes to about 40 GB. Where 96 GB of counter space goes vLLM, the open-source software that actually runs the model, takes 90% of each card’s memory by default. On one card, the 96 GB splits like this. 96 GB card x 0.9 vLLM's default share (leaves ~10 GB in reserve) = ~86 GB - 40 GB model weights (NVFP4) - 5 GB working memory while the model runs = ~41 GB left for order tickets (KV cache), per card x 4 cards = ~165 GB for the server On real servers, 4-bit storage holds about 1.7 times as many tokens as FP8, not a full 2x, because of that bookkeeping. The NVFP4 row below uses 1.7. How tickets are stored 8K conversations that fit 32K conversations ---------------------- ------------------------- ----------------- BF16 (16-bit) 61 15 FP8 (8-bit) 123 30 NVFP4 (4-bit) 208 52 Those are totals for the whole server, and each card holds a quarter. At 32K in FP8, one card has room for 7 conversations. All three formats clear the 30-person line easily. Only 4-bit storage reaches 200, the line where every employee’s conversation stays in memory at once. How many people actually get served Memory decides how many chats the server can keep open. Speed decides how many it can answer at the same moment. A chat sitting in memory while its owner reads takes up counter space but no cooking. NVIDIA publishes speed numbers for its own serving software, TensorRT-LLM, including Llama 3.3 70B in 4-bit on this exact card. They show the most the card can produce if nobody minds how long they wait. Short question, long answer (1,000 tokens in, 1,000 out): 1,724 tokens/s per card, enough for about 85 people Typical request (8,192 in, 1,024 out): 296 tokens/s per card, about 15 people Pasted contract (32,768 in, 1,024 out): 67 tokens/s per card, under a quarter of the typical figure Going from 1K to 8K of input cuts speed by more than 80%. Most of that is prefill, the chef reading a long order before cooking anything. Four copies at 296 tokens/s give you about 1,180 tokens/s, or 60 people at 20 tokens/s each. Treat 60 as the ceiling for NVIDIA’s engine, because it assumes nobody minds waiting. A GPU cooks for many tables in one batch, and the bigger the batch, the longer everyone waits for their first word. Keeping the first word under 2 seconds means smaller batches, so I plan on 30 to 50 people. The example needs 30, the bottom of that range, so one server is enough.Everything in the shaded band fits in memory and still waits too long. Long requests hurt fast. At 32K of input, throughput per card falls to under a quarter of the 8K figure, so a server fielding mostly long requests serves far fewer than 30 people at once. If a third of your requests look like that, capacity roughly halves, so plan a second server or a smaller model. Before you accept the server, run vllm bench serve on it with your real request lengths, at 8, 16, 32 and 64 people and with the power cap you'll run in production. Watch the first-word time as closely as the throughput. Keeping everyone’s conversation warm Two hundred people with 8K of context each is 1.64 million tokens, about a dozen novels’ worth of text held open at once. FP8 holds about 1.01 million across the server, so the system keeps clearing the tickets of people who stepped away for coffee. NVFP4 holds about 1.70 million, enough for everyone on paper, but only if the load balancer spreads people evenly. Spec: 12 x 64 GB DDR5 = 768 GB. Why: Overflow shelf for the cache. GPU. Spec: 4x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. Why: Four copies, capped at 450 W. Boot. Spec: 2x 960 GB NVMe, mirrored. items.summary_html:
How many users a GPU server really serves, and why memory alone gives the wrong answer

Almost every private LLM request I get in presales opens with “which GPU should we buy?” I start somewhere duller. How many people will use it at once, how much text will they paste in, and how long will they wait for a reply?

Take a company that wants its own AI assistant for 200 employees, running on its own hardware instead of a cloud API. Answer those questions and you land on one server with four GPUs, the chips that do the model’s math. That server has enough memory for well over 100 conversations, but I size it to handle only 30 to 50 at once.

An LLM server is a restaurant kitchen

The GPU is the kitchen. Its memory is the counter space.

The chef’s recipe book stays on that counter all the time. That’s the model’s weights, the numbers it learned during training.

Each diner who is still eating has an order ticket pinned there too, and the ticket gets longer as the conversation goes on. In LLM terms, that ticket is the KV cache. It holds the model’s notes on everything already said in the conversation, so it doesn’t have to re-read the whole chat for every new word. While the ticket stays pinned up, the conversation is warm. Clear it, and the chef has to read the whole order again from the top.

Throughput is how fast the kitchen cooks, measured in tokens per second. A token is about three-quarters of a word. Reading the order before cooking is called prefill, and a long order takes a while to read.

What “200 users” really means

Everything below comes from four numbers. If you can get only one of them from your logs, get the first.

  • People getting an answer at the same moment. Value for this example: 30 (15% of 200). Why it matters: How busy the kitchen is.
  • Typical request length. Value for this example: 8K tokens, about 6,000 words. Why it matters: Ticket size and reading time.
  • Worst case. Value for this example: 32K tokens, someone pastes a contract. Why it matters: The request that breaks your sizing.
  • What “served” means. Value for this example: First word within 2 s (engineers call it TTFT, time to first token), then at least 20 tokens/s. Why it matters: Smooth streaming, several times faster than most people read.

15% is generous for an internal assistant. Your chat logs, or the API gateway that sits in front of the model, will show you the real peak.

The model is Llama 3.3 70B. It’s a big open model, its specs are public, and NVIDIA has benchmarked it on the exact card I’m sizing.I work top to bottom in that funnel, and the GPU doesn’t show up until the last row.

The size of one conversation in memory

For every token the model has seen, it keeps a small record in GPU memory, one per layer. A layer is one of the model’s stacked processing steps.

How big that record is depends on precision, the number of bits each stored number gets. Fewer bits make a smaller ticket and a slightly less exact one. There are three common choices: BF16 at 16 bits, FP8 at 8 bits, and NVFP4 at 4 bits plus a little bookkeeping.

KV bytes per token = 2 (keys and values) x layers x KV heads x head_dim x bytes per number

Llama 3.3 70B’s spec file, config.json, is public and lists 80 layers, 8 KV heads and a head dimension of 128. The last two set how wide each record is. At 16 bits per number (BF16), each token costs 327,680 bytes, or 320 KiB, about a third of a megabyte. FP8 halves that to 160 KiB, and NVFP4 brings it down to about 94 KiB in practice, because of the bookkeeping bits.

So one 8K-token conversation is a 2.7 GB ticket at BF16 and 1.3 GB at FP8. Thirty people at 8K each puts about 245,000 tokens in memory at once, roughly 40 GB of counter space at FP8. At 32K, those thirty conversations need about 160 GB. That’s almost the entire cache budget of the server I end up with, eaten by thirty people pasting contracts.

Four cards, four copies

The GPU here is the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. It has 96 GB of memory, so four of them give you 384 GB of counter space. It reads that memory at about 1.6 TB/s, and that speed mostly decides how fast it writes each new word. You can cap its power anywhere between 400 W and 600 W.

These cards have no NVLink, NVIDIA’s fast private link between GPUs. They talk to each other over PCIe, the ordinary connection between the CPU and everything plugged into the motherboard, and PCIe is far slower.

You could split one copy of the model across all four cards. That’s called tensor parallelism, and it keeps the cards swapping data over that slow link all the time. I’d rather run four separate copies, one per card, and put a load balancer in front to decide which copy answers which person. Each copy is called a replica.

That only works if the model fits on one card. Llama 3.3 70B has 70.6 billion weights. Squeeze each one down to about 4.5 bits, which is called quantization (here using NVFP4), and the whole model comes to about 40 GB.

Where 96 GB of counter space goes

vLLM, the open-source software that actually runs the model, takes 90% of each card’s memory by default. On one card, the 96 GB splits like this.

96 GB card
 x 0.9   vLLM's default share (leaves ~10 GB in reserve)  = ~86 GB
 - 40 GB model weights (NVFP4)
 -  5 GB working memory while the model runs
 = ~41 GB left for order tickets (KV cache), per card
 x 4 cards                                                 = ~165 GB for the server

On real servers, 4-bit storage holds about 1.7 times as many tokens as FP8, not a full 2x, because of that bookkeeping. The NVFP4 row below uses 1.7.

How tickets are stored   8K conversations that fit   32K conversations
----------------------   -------------------------   -----------------
BF16 (16-bit)            61                          15
FP8 (8-bit)              123                         30
NVFP4 (4-bit)            208                         52

Those are totals for the whole server, and each card holds a quarter. At 32K in FP8, one card has room for 7 conversations.

All three formats clear the 30-person line easily. Only 4-bit storage reaches 200, the line where every employee’s conversation stays in memory at once.

How many people actually get served

Memory decides how many chats the server can keep open. Speed decides how many it can answer at the same moment. A chat sitting in memory while its owner reads takes up counter space but no cooking.

NVIDIA publishes speed numbers for its own serving software, TensorRT-LLM, including Llama 3.3 70B in 4-bit on this exact card. They show the most the card can produce if nobody minds how long they wait.

  • Short question, long answer (1,000 tokens in, 1,000 out): 1,724 tokens/s per card, enough for about 85 people
  • Typical request (8,192 in, 1,024 out): 296 tokens/s per card, about 15 people
  • Pasted contract (32,768 in, 1,024 out): 67 tokens/s per card, under a quarter of the typical figure

Going from 1K to 8K of input cuts speed by more than 80%. Most of that is prefill, the chef reading a long order before cooking anything.

Four copies at 296 tokens/s give you about 1,180 tokens/s, or 60 people at 20 tokens/s each. Treat 60 as the ceiling for NVIDIA’s engine, because it assumes nobody minds waiting. A GPU cooks for many tables in one batch, and the bigger the batch, the longer everyone waits for their first word. Keeping the first word under 2 seconds means smaller batches, so I plan on 30 to 50 people. The example needs 30, the bottom of that range, so one server is enough.Everything in the shaded band fits in memory and still waits too long.

Long requests hurt fast. At 32K of input, throughput per card falls to under a quarter of the 8K figure, so a server fielding mostly long requests serves far fewer than 30 people at once. If a third of your requests look like that, capacity roughly halves, so plan a second server or a smaller model.

Before you accept the server, run vllm bench serve on it with your real request lengths, at 8, 16, 32 and 64 people and with the power cap you'll run in production. Watch the first-word time as closely as the throughput.

Keeping everyone’s conversation warm

Two hundred people with 8K of context each is 1.64 million tokens, about a dozen novels’ worth of text held open at once. FP8 holds about 1.01 million across the server, so the system keeps clearing the tickets of people who stepped away for coffee. NVFP4 holds about 1.70 million, enough for everyone on paper, but only if the load balancer spreads people evenly. A warm conversation skips the expensive reading step, so its first word arrives much sooner.

With four copies, the ticket only helps if the person’s next message goes to the copy that holds it. So the load balancer has to send each person back to the same copy every time. Engineers call this session affinity, and some routers do it by matching the start of the prompt (prefix-aware routing). Plain round-robin, where each new request just goes to the next copy in line, sends about three out of four follow-ups to a copy that doesn’t have the ticket. That copy reads the whole order again.

4-bit storage also helps with the rare very long requests. FP8 fits about 30 of them across the server, 7 per card. NVFP4 fits about 52, or 13 per card, so the server holds 22 more long conversations before it has to pause some of them to make room.

vLLM added 4-bit KV cache for this generation of GPU in v0.32.0, released on 18 October 2026. You turn it on with the --kv-cache-dtype option. NVIDIA reports under 1% accuracy loss compared with 8-bit and 16-bit storage. Run your own documents through it before rollout.

To a buyer, I pitch 4-bit storage as “everyone’s conversation stays warm”, not “more users per server”.

The model matters as much as the GPU

In the same NVIDIA table, on the same card and the same 8K-request test, Qwen3–30B-A3B in 4-bit produces 1,914 tokens/s. Llama 3.3 70B produces 296. That’s about 95 people instead of 15, six times the users, just from changing the model.

The difference comes from how Qwen3–30B-A3B is built. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with about 30 billion weights, but only about 3 billion of them do any work for a given token. Picture the same kitchen with 128 specialist cooks, where for each word only the 8 best suited step in. You still need counter space for all 128, but each word cooks much faster.

So I’d test a 30B-class model like this one first. If it does your real work well enough, size the hardware for it. If it handles only some of it, keep the 70B for the rest.

How a model is built changes its memory needs too. OpenAI’s gpt-oss-120b has 36 layers, and half of them only look at the last 128 tokens instead of the whole conversation. So in a long chat, its ticket costs about 36 KiB per token at BF16, nine times as many conversations per gigabyte as Llama 70B. But its weights alone take about 60 GB of counter space before a single ticket goes up. Read the spec file of the model you’ll actually run before you borrow anyone’s numbers.

The rest of the server

The rest comes down to lanes and watts. PCIe is split into lanes, individual data connections, and each device gets a fixed number of them. Four GPUs at 16 lanes each need 64. One AMD EPYC 9005 processor has 128 PCIe Gen5 lanes. That covers the four GPUs, four NVMe drives (fast SSDs) at 4 lanes each and a 16-lane network card, with 32 lanes left over. A second CPU buys you nothing here.

For system memory, put a stick on each of the CPU’s 12 memory channels, its parallel paths to RAM, so it gets full bandwidth. I default to 768 GB (12 x 64 GB), about twice the GPU memory. Models load fast, and tickets that don’t fit on the GPUs get an overflow shelf in system RAM.

Storage is simple. Mirror two boot drives so the server still boots if one dies, and add two 7.68 TB NVMe drives for model versions and for cache that spills to disk. Two 25 GbE network ports are plenty for a server that only sends and receives text.

Power is the line that’s easiest to get wrong. Four cards at 600 W is 2,400 W. Budget about 500 W for the CPU, memory, drives and fans, and the server draws roughly 2.9 kW at full load. Cap each card at 450 W and the GPUs draw 1,800 W, the whole server about 2.3 kW. That is about 10 A at 230 V, running around the clock.

Then size the power supplies so either one can carry that load alone, with room to spare. That’s what redundant means here: one supply fails and the server keeps running. Get the supply’s peak-load rating in writing, and confirm your rack can deliver 3 kW and cool it.The finished bill of materials

If you check only two rows, check GPU and Power. The power cap sets how much the server draws, and each supply has to carry that draw alone.

  • CPU. Spec: 1x AMD EPYC 9005, mid core count. Why: 128 lanes, 12 memory channels.
  • Memory. Spec: 12 x 64 GB DDR5 = 768 GB. Why: Overflow shelf for the cache.
  • GPU. Spec: 4x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. Why: Four copies, capped at 450 W.
  • Boot. Spec: 2x 960 GB NVMe, mirrored. Why: Operating system.
  • Data. Spec: 2x 7.68 TB NVMe. Why: Model versions, disk cache.
  • Network. Spec: 2x 25 GbE. Why: Text in, text out.
  • Power. Spec: Redundant supplies, each rated at 3 kW or more. Why: Either supply carries the whole server alone.
Before anyone signs the quote
  • Write down how many people at once you’re sizing for, and where that number came from.
  • Pull the 95th-percentile request length (the length only 1 request in 20 exceeds) from your logs.
  • Decide how each person gets sent back to the same copy every time.
  • Test a 30B-class model against the 70B on your real tasks before fixing the GPU count.
  • Get the GPU power cap written into the quote, and check that one power supply alone can carry the whole server.
  • Agree who runs the speed test on the delivered server, with your own prompts, before you accept it.

How does your team decide how many people will use it at once? If you have real usage logs from an internal assistant, I’d like to compare notes.

If this resonated and you want to go deeper on the technical side, the architecture decisions, the infra tradeoffs and the detail that doesn’t fit in a blog post, connect with me on LinkedIn. I’m always up for a good conversation about the unglamorous reality of building AI systems that actually work.

items.title: iOS 27.3 Beta Brings Face Unlock to the iPhone Duo, but It Cannot Approve Apple Pay
items.summary: Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo, its first folding iPhone, in the second developer beta of iOS 27.3. The iPhone Duo shipped with Touch ID instead of Face ID, because the hinge and display layers leave no room for the TrueDepth sensor that Face ID needs. It is the first new iPhone with Touch ID since the third generation iPhone SE. The new feature is not Face ID. Apple is borrowing the person recognition technology from its HomeView smart display, which uses its camera to recognize up to six people in a household. How iPhone Duo Face Unlock Works Face unlock on the iPhone Duo is protected by the Secure Exclave, a memory protected space in the A20 Pro processor, and not by the Secure Enclave chip that stores Face ID data. It is less comprehensive than Face ID and could be more open to attacks. Apple limits it in these ways: it only unlocks the phone and cannot approve Apple Pay or Apple Wallet purchases passwords and sensitive content, such as banking apps, still need Touch ID or the passcode it needs a Touch ID or passcode unlock within the last 45 minutes it works only with the front screen and camera, not when the Duo is unfolded Face unlock is off by default. Users who want it can turn it on: Install the iOS 27.3 beta, or iOS 27.3 once it is released. Open Settings and go to Touch ID & Passcode. Turn on the face unlock option. Lock the iPhone Duo by Closing It iOS 27.3 also adds an option to lock the iPhone Duo when it is folded shut. Until now, closing the phone did not lock it, and users had to press the side button to put it to sleep. The new setting is optional, so users who want to move between folded and unfolded modes without locking the phone can leave it off. It is under Settings, then Display & Brightness. The update brings other changes for all iPhones, including the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions. Developers and public testers can install the beta now. The current public release is iOS 27.2.1, which Apple released last week to fix security vulnerabilities and bugs, including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they should not have access to. Among folding phones sold in the US, only Google's newer Pixel foldables offer secure facial authentication. Samsung's face recognition on Galaxy phones is not strong enough to protect sensitive content and is mainly used to unlock the device. Apple has not announced a release date for iOS 27.3. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo, its first folding iPhone, in the second developer beta of iOS 27.3. The iPhone Duo shipped with Touch ID instead of Face ID, because the hinge and display layers leave no room for the TrueDepth sensor that Face ID needs. It is the first new iPhone with Touch ID since the third generation iPhone SE.

The new feature is not Face ID. Apple is borrowing the person recognition technology from its HomeView smart display, which uses its camera to recognize up to six people in a household.

How iPhone Duo Face Unlock Works

Face unlock on the iPhone Duo is protected by the Secure Exclave, a memory protected space in the A20 Pro processor, and not by the Secure Enclave chip that stores Face ID data. It is less comprehensive than Face ID and could be more open to attacks. Apple limits it in these ways:

  • it only unlocks the phone and cannot approve Apple Pay or Apple Wallet purchases
  • passwords and sensitive content, such as banking apps, still need Touch ID or the passcode
  • it needs a Touch ID or passcode unlock within the last 45 minutes
  • it works only with the front screen and camera, not when the Duo is unfolded

Face unlock is off by default. Users who want it can turn it on:

  1. Install the iOS 27.3 beta, or iOS 27.3 once it is released.
  2. Open Settings and go to Touch ID & Passcode.
  3. Turn on the face unlock option.
Lock the iPhone Duo by Closing It

iOS 27.3 also adds an option to lock the iPhone Duo when it is folded shut. Until now, closing the phone did not lock it, and users had to press the side button to put it to sleep. The new setting is optional, so users who want to move between folded and unfolded modes without locking the phone can leave it off. It is under Settings, then Display & Brightness.

The update brings other changes for all iPhones, including the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions. Developers and public testers can install the beta now. The current public release is iOS 27.2.1, which Apple released last week to fix security vulnerabilities and bugs, including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they should not have access to.

Among folding phones sold in the US, only Google's newer Pixel foldables offer secure facial authentication. Samsung's face recognition on Galaxy phones is not strong enough to protect sensitive content and is mainly used to unlock the device.

items.title: Neo4j in FastAPI
items.summary: Neo4j and FastAPI Neo4j is a native graph database. It stores and represents data in graph format through nodes and relationships ( aka links ). The relationships have directions and mark source & destination nodes. These nodes and relationships have one or more properties associated with them.
