items.summary_html:
Neo4j and FastAPI

Neo4j is a native graph database. It stores and represents data in graph format through nodes and relationships (aka links). The relationships have directions and mark source & destination nodes. These nodes and relationships have one or more properties associated with them. Neo4j also has most of the capabilities of a traditional database. You can define constraints & indexes, execute transactions, run subqueries, etc. You can also integrate Neo4j with RAG systems to provide structured context.

Read more about Neo4j

FastAPI is a modern and ‘fast’ web framework for building APIs with Python. It supports automatic documentation creation and follows OpenAPI standards. You can easily implement validations and enjoy unlimited plugins.

Read more about FastAPI

In a traditional backend system, when an API is triggered, it generally makes a query in the database and returns the result. A similar architecture can be implemented with FastAPI as the backend framework and Neo4j as the database. Here, you’ll implement multiple HTTP APIs to perform different operations in Neo4j.

Prerequisite
  1. Neo4j Aura DB details (URI, Database Name, Username & Password).
  2. Python 3.14.9 virtual environment
Basic Implementation of FastAPIhttps://medium.com/media/36e3f27b3d23c2350b31493bb433dfd4/href

i. Import the required packages.

ii. Initialize the FastAPI app.

iii. Configure middleware for APIs

iv. Create a GET API

v. Start the server

How to start the server-

i. Save the file with the name main.py (or any other name).

ii. Open the terminal and initialize the Python virtual environment.

# Create virtual environment with the name ".venv"
python -m venv .venv

# Activate the virtual environment
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat

iii. Run the command below to install the required packages listed in requirements.txt file.

pip install -r requirements.txt

You can find a suitable requirements.txt file at this link.

iv. Once the packages are installed, run the server file. Although you can run the server with python main.py, an improvement could be to use fastapi dev. This will start your server in development mode. You can also access the interactive API documentation provided by SwaggerUI.

fastapi dev

v. This will start your server locally on port 8000. Open http://localhost:8000/docs to access the automatically created interactive documentation.

Establish a connection with the Neo4j Instance

i. Import the required packages from Neo4j and provide database details & credentials to initialize the driver instance. You can find the database details on the Neo4j Aura Instance page.

from neo4j import GraphDatabase

# Connect to Neo4j database
NEO4J_URI = '...'
NEO4J_USERNAME = '...'
NEO4J_PASSWORD = '...'
NEO4J_DATABASE= '...'

# Initialize the driver
driver = GraphDatabase.driver(
    NEO4J_URI, 
    auth=(
        NEO4J_USERNAME, 
        NEO4J_PASSWORD
    )
)

ii. With the database driver initialized, call the built-in verify_connectivity() method to verify the database connection. You should perform this verification inside the main block. You can also put the code to start the server inside the same main block.

def verify_neo4j_connection():
    global driver
    try:
        driver.verify_connectivity()
        return "Neo4j verify connection successful."
    except:
        driver.close()
        return "Neo4j verify connection failed. Check the NEO4J_URI, NEO4J_USERNAME, and NEO4J_PASSWORD values in .env file."


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Verify Neo4j Connection
    conn_status = verify_neo4j_connection()
    print("Status: ", conn_status)

    # Run local server
    import uvicorn
    uvicorn.run("main:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, reload=True)

Next, you need to implement APIs and make queries to the Neo4j database.

APIs with Neo4j Queries

i. Create a GET API (“/customer/all”)

ii. Create a function that will be called when this API is triggered

iii. Inside the defined function, execute a query that will fetch the list of names of Customers who have Placed an Order. The execute_query() method of the Neo4j driver is used to execute queries. It takes a minimum of two parameters: the query and the database name. You can also create the query with dynamic values by passing them as additional parameters to the execute_query() method.

iv. The API will return the customer name list.

The Neo4j driver supports queries in the Cypher query language. It is close to natural language and visually matches the patterns and relationships in its syntax.

Read more about Cypher

# Get All Customers
@app.get("/customer/all")
def get_all_customers():
    try:
        # Use Neo4j driver and execute query
        # Below query will fetch the list of names of customers who haved placed an order
        # -> Nodes: Customer, Order
        # -> Relationship: Placed
        records, summary, keys = driver.execute_query("""
            MATCH (c:Customer)-[:PLACED]->(:Order)
            RETURN c.name AS name
            """,
            database_=NEO4J_DATABASE,
        )

        # Loop through results and do something with them
        for record in records:
            print(record.data())  # obtain record as dict

        # Summary information
        print("The query `{query}` returned {records_count} records in {time} ms.".format(
            query=summary.query, records_count=len(records),
            time=summary.result_available_after
        ))

        # Return the query response
        return records
    except:
        return {'error': 'Something went wrong'}
Call the API

Once the above changes are done, you can visit http://localhost:8000/docs and trigger the ‘customer/all’ API from the interactive UI. It will return a list of customer names.

SwaggerUI DocumentationClose the Database Driver

Database drivers are resource-intensive. Unless you really need it, initialize only a single instance of the database driver. Also, when the server stops, properly release all resources, including the database driver.

You can implement driver-closing logic inside the FastAPI shutdown event listener.

# FastAPI 'shutdown' Event
@app.on_event("shutdown")
async def shutdown_event():
    # close the database driver
    driver.close()
    print('Neo4j Driver Closed')

After completing the above-discussed steps, your main.py file will look something like this-

https://medium.com/media/40dbe7d0e7354642aa71f25e751b3dff/hrefFew More APIsGet Customer

Get details of the customer with the provided name who has placed an order. The API will return all the details of the customer.

# Get Customer
@app.get("/customer/")
def get_customer(name: str = 'George'):
    try:
        records, summary, keys = driver.execute_query("""
            MATCH (c:Customer {name: $name})-[:PLACED]->(:Order)
            RETURN c
            """, name=name,
            database_=NEO4J_DATABASE,
        )

        # Summary information
        print("The query `{query}` returned {records_count} records in {time} ms.".format(
            query=summary.query, records_count=len(records),
            time=summary.result_available_after
        ))
        return records
    except:
        return {'error': 'Something went wrong'}
Update Customer

Update the email of the customer with the provided name who has placed an order. The API will return a success message.

# Update Customer
@app.put("/customer")
def update_customer(name: str = 'George', email: str = 'George_Anderson62@yahoo.com'):
    try:
        records, summary, keys = driver.execute_query("""
            MATCH (c:Customer {name: $name})
            SET c.email = $email
            """, name=name, email=email,
            database_=NEO4J_DATABASE,
        )
        print(f"Query counters: {summary.counters}.")
        return {'status': 'success'}
    except:
        return {'error': 'Something went wrong'}
Create Customer

Create a new customer with the provided name & email. Since this customer will be newly created, it won’t have any relationships like :PLACED, etc. The API will return the count of nodes (customers) created.

# Create Customer
@app.post("/customer")
def post_customer(name: str, email: str):
    try:
        joined_date = datetime.now()
        customer_id = f"customer{random.randrange(100,1000)}"
        records, summary, keys = driver.execute_query("""
            CREATE (c:Customer {name: $name, email: $email, joinedDate: $joined_date, customerId: $customer_id})
            """, name=name, email=email, joined_date=joined_date,customer_id=customer_id,
            database_=NEO4J_DATABASE,
        )

        print("Created {nodes_created} nodes in {time} ms.".format(
            nodes_created=summary.counters.nodes_created,
            time=summary.result_available_after
        ))

        return {'nodes': summary.counters.nodes_created}
    except:
        return {'error': 'Something went wrong'}
Delete Customer

Delete the customer with the provided name and all its relationships. The API will return the count of nodes deleted.

# Delete Customer
@app.delete("/customer")
def delete_customer(name: str):
    try:
        records, summary, keys = driver.execute_query("""
        MATCH (c:Customer {name: $name})
        DETACH DELETE c
        """, name=name,
        database_=NEO4J_DATABASE)

        print("Deleted {nodes_deleted} nodes in {time} ms.".format(
            nodes_deleted=summary.counters.nodes_deleted,
            time=summary.result_available_after
        ))

        return {'nodes': summary.counters.nodes_created}
    except:
        return {'error': 'Something went wrong'}

These are just some very simple examples of different HTTP methods and how they can be integrated with the Neo4j database. There are still an enormous number of features to be explored.

Visit Neo4j Docs and learn more!

Check out my git repo: Neo4j — FastAPI Integration

items.title: Nvidia’s Board Should Come Clean on Huang’s Resignation
items.summary: Memo to the board of Nvidia: Folks, you need to explain why you pressured Jensen Huang to resign. Otherwise, a bring-back-Jensen movement will only grow and could theoretically escalate to the point where it threatens your roles on Nvidia’s board. Even President Donald Trump has weighed in, supporting Huang. The board could use Nvidia’s earnings update on Tuesday to provide everyone with some answers. As quixotic as the Jensen loyalists’ effort may seem right now, some of their complaints are on the money. A letter from investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker posted on X on Friday, for instance, made the point that there was “massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding” Huang’s departure. The pair were correct to say that a “slow, measured and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia” was in everyone’s best interests.

items.title: I'm the CEO of Klook. I spend my free time scrolling through customer complaint emails — and Hyrox training.
items.summary: Klook This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ethan Lin, the 40-year-old cofounder and CEO of travel platform Klook, who is based in Hong Kong. The following has been edited for length and clarity. In 2014, I left a stable banking job to cofound Klook, a platform where people can book travel experiences. I was 27, had no experience in tech or product, and bootstrapped the business with the savings my cofounders and I had built up. Now, the company is almost 2,000 employees-strong across 25 offices. As a 40-year-old CEO, I spend most of my time on work and fitness. Here's how I bring my A-game on busy work days. Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful people structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. An 8 a.m. dopamine boost Fitness is really important to me. It's a dopamine boost in the morning; it works better than coffee. Each week, I go to the gym five to six times, mostly in the morning before work, around 7 or 8 a.m. That helps me wake up. I have a light meal, and then I hit the gym for some strength training. I participated in Hyrox in Bangkok a few weeks ago. Klook is Hyrox's travel partner across Asia, and I like to show support. After my morning workout, I have a light meal that helps me start the day feeling very energetic. I reach the office around 9 a.m., then AI automations help me kick off I have several AI projects in the works that help me keep on top of my game. I have an AI automation set up that sends me a weekly Monday morning summary email, giving me a quick refresh on what's happening each week. Other AI automations work like think tanks for me, acting like a consultant, industry expert, communication strategist, analyst, and so on, brainstorming with me. One thing I enjoy about AI is that it feels like you're working with many experts every day. When it comes to drafting emails, I feed AI the skeletons of the content and structure and let it write a draft for me because English isn't my first language, but the critical thinking and judgment have to come from me. I need to remind myself to be mindful because they all sound right, and I need to be the one deciding what information is really suitable for me. Before AI, when you worked on a project or task or sent emails, you would get a few hours or days of break before you got a response, or the next piece of information. Right now, that part is pretty much instant, so we end up basically working nonstop. I feel like I'm being mentally challenged more and more every day. I scroll through customer complaint emails — and enjoy reading them I'm copied on all Klook customer inquiry or complaint email chains, and I enjoy reading them every day as they come in. In the last 12 years, that's one habit I haven't changed. The emails often look like: "I booked a day for this activity, but can I change to another day? The system doesn't support it," or "I wrote my name wrong. Can I get entry into this venue without the right name? Can you change it?" It's something AI can help summarize, but I like to get them randomly every day, even on weekends, because you cannot predict when a customer will submit a complaint. It's like TikTok — swipe, swipe, you never know what's coming next. It's quite addictive. I don't respond directly to them — that would be a bit awkward — but scrolling through complaints gives me enough frequent data points and real case studies to get a sense of our customers' problems. When we actually conduct analyses or prioritize which problems to solve, I have enough tangible examples. I'm in the office until at least 7 p.m. Most days, I'm in the office until 7 to 8 p.m., although other days can get quite late. That's also why I try to protect my morning workouts to kick-start the day, as my evening workouts aren't guaranteed. As a CEO, my time is very fragmented : I spend half an hour on one task, 15 minutes on another, and an hour on something else. I get sucked into a lot of projects and meetings but often don't have time to sit and think about how they're linked to see if anything's missing. Every week, I block off two to three hours from my calendar for personal reflection. I'll use that to finish a project or task, or consolidate information. My second workout, followed by bed at 1 a.m. After work, about twice a week at night, I hit cardio. I do a light zone-two run . That means a four- to eight-kilometer run at a not-too-crazy pace, depending on how busy my day has been. This helps me build endurance and sleep better, although I'm already a pretty deep sleeper. The last hour or so of my day is my quiet time. This involves some email clean-up, prepping for the next day, and reading things outside technology and travel to give myself a different perspective. I'm normally asleep by 1 a.m. Read the original article on Business Insider

Klook

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ethan Lin, the 40-year-old cofounder and CEO of travel platform Klook, who is based in Hong Kong. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

In 2014, I left a stable banking job to cofound Klook, a platform where people can book travel experiences.

I was 27, had no experience in tech or product, and bootstrapped the business with the savings my cofounders and I had built up. Now, the company is almost 2,000 employees-strong across 25 offices.

As a 40-year-old CEO, I spend most of my time on work and fitness. Here's how I bring my A-game on busy work days.

Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful people structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine.

An 8 a.m. dopamine boost

Fitness is really important to me. It's a dopamine boost in the morning; it works better than coffee.

Each week, I go to the gym five to six times, mostly in the morning before work, around 7 or 8 a.m. That helps me wake up.

I have a light meal, and then I hit the gym for some strength training. I participated in Hyrox in Bangkok a few weeks ago. Klook is Hyrox's travel partner across Asia, and I like to show support.

After my morning workout, I have a light meal that helps me start the day feeling very energetic.

I reach the office around 9 a.m., then AI automations help me kick off

I have several AI projects in the works that help me keep on top of my game.

I have an AI automation set up that sends me a weekly Monday morning summary email, giving me a quick refresh on what's happening each week.

Other AI automations work like think tanks for me, acting like a consultant, industry expert, communication strategist, analyst, and so on, brainstorming with me. One thing I enjoy about AI is that it feels like you're working with many experts every day.

When it comes to drafting emails, I feed AI the skeletons of the content and structure and let it write a draft for me because English isn't my first language, but the critical thinking and judgment have to come from me.

I need to remind myself to be mindful because they all sound right, and I need to be the one deciding what information is really suitable for me.

Before AI, when you worked on a project or task or sent emails, you would get a few hours or days of break before you got a response, or the next piece of information. Right now, that part is pretty much instant, so we end up basically working nonstop. I feel like I'm being mentally challenged more and more every day.

I scroll through customer complaint emails — and enjoy reading them

I'm copied on all Klook customer inquiry or complaint email chains, and I enjoy reading them every day as they come in. In the last 12 years, that's one habit I haven't changed.

The emails often look like: "I booked a day for this activity, but can I change to another day? The system doesn't support it," or "I wrote my name wrong. Can I get entry into this venue without the right name? Can you change it?"

It's something AI can help summarize, but I like to get them randomly every day, even on weekends, because you cannot predict when a customer will submit a complaint. It's like TikTok — swipe, swipe, you never know what's coming next. It's quite addictive.

I don't respond directly to them — that would be a bit awkward — but scrolling through complaints gives me enough frequent data points and real case studies to get a sense of our customers' problems. When we actually conduct analyses or prioritize which problems to solve, I have enough tangible examples.

I'm in the office until at least 7 p.m.

Most days, I'm in the office until 7 to 8 p.m., although other days can get quite late. That's also why I try to protect my morning workouts to kick-start the day, as my evening workouts aren't guaranteed.

As a CEO, my time is very fragmented: I spend half an hour on one task, 15 minutes on another, and an hour on something else. I get sucked into a lot of projects and meetings but often don't have time to sit and think about how they're linked to see if anything's missing.

Every week, I block off two to three hours from my calendar for personal reflection. I'll use that to finish a project or task, or consolidate information.

My second workout, followed by bed at 1 a.m.

After work, about twice a week at night, I hit cardio. I do a light zone-two run. That means a four- to eight-kilometer run at a not-too-crazy pace, depending on how busy my day has been. This helps me build endurance and sleep better, although I'm already a pretty deep sleeper.

The last hour or so of my day is my quiet time. This involves some email clean-up, prepping for the next day, and reading things outside technology and travel to give myself a different perspective.

I'm normally asleep by 1 a.m.

items.title: Two camps emerge in Silicon Valley: For Jensen Huang, or against
items.summary: Lisi Niesner/Reuters; BI Silicon Valley is divided over Jensen Huang, following his resignation over his infidelity. Some tech leaders, such as former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, want Huang back in charge at Nvidia. Huang is more controversial in the AI community, and with some women in tech. Where do you stand on Jensen ? That question is roiling Silicon Valley as it reckons with the tech titan's fall from grace. Venture capitalists, tech founders, and Nvidia employees are rallying to his defense — and some are pushing to bring him back. But others see the rush to forgive him as a familiar Silicon Valley reflex: excusing a powerful man's conduct while minimizing the damage to the people and institutions around him. The Nvidia cofounder and CEO resigned last week following reports that he had multiple affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and a subordinate. To some, that's overshadowed by his achievements. "Jensen is one of the great builders of our time. We cannot starve the future of his innovation and industrial breakthroughs," reads a comment from Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick on Stand With Jensen , an online petition with more than 186,000 signatures. "To err is human," Kalanick — who said he is crowdsourcing "wild ideas" to get Huang reinstated — added. Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider on Monday. Kalanick joins a growing chorus of people in tech defending Huang, including Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Nvidia executives, all of whom have signed the petition. For others, Huang's downfall was well-deserved given the ethical and national security implications of his conduct. Huang has long rankled some corners of tech because of his constant lobbying to sell powerful AI chips to China. One notable venture investor privately disagreed with Huang's friendly approach to China, given the chronic chip shortage in the US. The investor was frustrated that Huang had done little to address the industry's growing compute crisis, with some startups struggling to secure the resources needed to continue scaling. Nvidia had a lot of compute primarily reserved for research and development, the person said. Huang's business tactics are being scrutinized more than ever given his relationship with one of Nvidia's biggest customers, who some in the US government believe was part of an espionage scheme. That's without even mentioning his reported affair with an employee, executive Kimberly Powell, while he painted himself as a family man. One woman VC said Huang's infidelity and potential national security implications have barely surfaced in her Silicon Valley women's group chats. Some women investors, she said, have expressed that they feel sorry for Huang's wife. But, she said, "The general sentiment is, 'He's such a great leader, who cares what he does in his private life?'" Another woman VC said she and other women in venture were hardly surprised by the news, having grown accustomed to such conduct in the Valley. "Any time there is ego, power, and money, this is what happens," she said. "The tech right and founder class is rallying behind Jensen against all reason," Zvi Mowshowitz, who publishes an influential AI Substack, told Business Insider. At stake isn't just whether Huang gets back on top of Nvidia or not — an unlikely prospect — but the legacy of a key figure behind the AI boom. The godfather of the AI boom For years, Nvidia was best known for the graphics cards it sold to PC gamers. Huang was prescient in predicting that the high-powered chips would power the AI revolution. In a fateful moment, he personally delivered an Nvidia supercomputer, the DGX-1, to OpenAI's office in 2016. It was signed by then-OpenAI researcher Dario Amodei, who now runs Anthropic — which is set for a trillion-dollar blockbuster IPO this week. Huang's role in helping birth the thriving AI startup ecosystem is partly why so many venture capitalists are still Huang fans, industry insiders said. Nvidia's rise has been lucrative for them, too. Nvidia often invested in AI startups at high valuations, boosting the value of their portfolio companies by the billions. The funding also benefited Nvidia because it could be used to buy even more Nvidia chips. If the next Nvidia CEO takes a less aggressive investment approach, it could be the beginning of an AI industry correction, some investors cautioned. Tatiana Koffman, a GP at Moonwalker Capital, said Nvidia's board should finish its investigation, and that Huang should be reinstated if it finds no credible proof of a security breach. "We're painting Jensen with a moral brush for something leaders have done time and time again. He's one of the greatest engineers of the last two generations, and few people have done more for American innovation," she said. A divided AI community In the AI policy and safety world, Huang's push to sell Nvidia chips to China raised concerns about giving a US competitor powerful AI hardware. As worries about AI going rogue reached a fever pitch, Huang's staunch defense of the technology also raised eyebrows. "I would say Jensen's views have been at odds with a lot of the AI community," said former OpenAI employee Will Depue. Huang's brash statements annoyed some of the most senior people in the industry. After Huang said that Anthropic was trying to control AI through safety regulations, Amodei called Huang's claim "the most outrageous lie I've ever heard." Lior Susan, founder and CEO of VC firm Eclipse — which has invested in startups that Nvidia has also backed, like autonomous driving company Wayve — said the industry will endure beyond any single man. “Jensen was huge for the industry of AI and robotics, but the rise of robotics did not happen because of one person, and the rapid technological transformations we are witnessing will not slow down,” Susan told Business Insider. “There is a world after Jensen, and there is still so much progress to be made.” Have a tip? items.summary_html:
Lisi Niesner/Reuters; BI

  • Silicon Valley is divided over Jensen Huang, following his resignation over his infidelity.
  • Some tech leaders, such as former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, want Huang back in charge at Nvidia.
  • Huang is more controversial in the AI community, and with some women in tech.

Where do you stand on Jensen?

That question is roiling Silicon Valley as it reckons with the tech titan's fall from grace.

Venture capitalists, tech founders, and Nvidia employees are rallying to his defense — and some are pushing to bring him back. But others see the rush to forgive him as a familiar Silicon Valley reflex: excusing a powerful man's conduct while minimizing the damage to the people and institutions around him.

The Nvidia cofounder and CEO resigned last week following reports that he had multiple affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and a subordinate. To some, that's overshadowed by his achievements.

"Jensen is one of the great builders of our time. We cannot starve the future of his innovation and industrial breakthroughs," reads a comment from Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick on Stand With Jensen, an online petition with more than 186,000 signatures.

"To err is human," Kalanick — who said he is crowdsourcing "wild ideas" to get Huang reinstated — added.

Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider on Monday.

Kalanick joins a growing chorus of people in tech defending Huang, including Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Nvidia executives, all of whom have signed the petition.

For others, Huang's downfall was well-deserved given the ethical and national security implications of his conduct. Huang has long rankled some corners of tech because of his constant lobbying to sell powerful AI chips to China.

One notable venture investor privately disagreed with Huang's friendly approach to China, given the chronic chip shortage in the US.

The investor was frustrated that Huang had done little to address the industry's growing compute crisis, with some startups struggling to secure the resources needed to continue scaling. Nvidia had a lot of compute primarily reserved for research and development, the person said.

Huang's business tactics are being scrutinized more than ever given his relationship with one of Nvidia's biggest customers, who some in the US government believe was part of an espionage scheme.

That's without even mentioning his reported affair with an employee, executive Kimberly Powell, while he painted himself as a family man.

One woman VC said Huang's infidelity and potential national security implications have barely surfaced in her Silicon Valley women's group chats. Some women investors, she said, have expressed that they feel sorry for Huang's wife. But, she said, "The general sentiment is, 'He's such a great leader, who cares what he does in his private life?'"

Another woman VC said she and other women in venture were hardly surprised by the news, having grown accustomed to such conduct in the Valley. "Any time there is ego, power, and money, this is what happens," she said.

"The tech right and founder class is rallying behind Jensen against all reason," Zvi Mowshowitz, who publishes an influential AI Substack, told Business Insider.

At stake isn't just whether Huang gets back on top of Nvidia or not — an unlikely prospect — but the legacy of a key figure behind the AI boom.

The godfather of the AI boom

For years, Nvidia was best known for the graphics cards it sold to PC gamers. Huang was prescient in predicting that the high-powered chips would power the AI revolution.

In a fateful moment, he personally delivered an Nvidia supercomputer, the DGX-1, to OpenAI's office in 2016. It was signed by then-OpenAI researcher Dario Amodei, who now runs Anthropic — which is set for a trillion-dollar blockbuster IPO this week.

Huang's role in helping birth the thriving AI startup ecosystem is partly why so many venture capitalists are still Huang fans, industry insiders said.

Nvidia's rise has been lucrative for them, too. Nvidia often invested in AI startups at high valuations, boosting the value of their portfolio companies by the billions.

The funding also benefited Nvidia because it could be used to buy even more Nvidia chips. If the next Nvidia CEO takes a less aggressive investment approach, it could be the beginning of an AI industry correction, some investors cautioned.

Tatiana Koffman, a GP at Moonwalker Capital, said Nvidia's board should finish its investigation, and that Huang should be reinstated if it finds no credible proof of a security breach.

"We're painting Jensen with a moral brush for something leaders have done time and time again. He's one of the greatest engineers of the last two generations, and few people have done more for American innovation," she said.

A divided AI community

In the AI policy and safety world, Huang's push to sell Nvidia chips to China raised concerns about giving a US competitor powerful AI hardware.

As worries about AI going rogue reached a fever pitch, Huang's staunch defense of the technology also raised eyebrows.

"I would say Jensen's views have been at odds with a lot of the AI community," said former OpenAI employee Will Depue.

Huang's brash statements annoyed some of the most senior people in the industry.

After Huang said that Anthropic was trying to control AI through safety regulations, Amodei called Huang's claim "the most outrageous lie I've ever heard."

Lior Susan, founder and CEO of VC firm Eclipse — which has invested in startups that Nvidia has also backed, like autonomous driving company Wayve — said the industry will endure beyond any single man.

“Jensen was huge for the industry of AI and robotics, but the rise of robotics did not happen because of one person, and the rapid technological transformations we are witnessing will not slow down,” Susan told Business Insider.

“There is a world after Jensen, and there is still so much progress to be made.”

items.title: Bill Ackman lays out how an activist investor effort to restore Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO could work
items.summary: Bill Ackman said he'd want to clarify the legal uncertainties around Jensen Huang's affairs before launching an activist campaign to restore him as Nvidia CEO. Godofredo A. Vásquez/AFP via Getty Images Investor Bill Ackman has defended Jensen Huang amid the scandals surrounding the former Nvidia CEO. Ackman said he believes there would be ample investor support for reinstating Huang. The case could be made if the legal uncertainties around Huang's affairs are cleared, he said. Bill Ackman said there could be a case for reinstating Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO — that is, only if Huang is cleared of any wrongdoing related to putting his company's national security obligations at risk. At a conference hosted by Semafor on Monday, the billionaire activist investor was asked what strategy he would use to pressure the board into reinstating Huang. Huang resigned from his role on Thursday following the disclosure of extramarital affairs and concerns that he may have been a target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Ackman said that if Huang's relationships were determined to be a "personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy," there could be a "powerful case" for putting Huang back in the CEO seat, though the investor said it would be "unlikely" for him to be involved in such an effort. "You just present the facts, and you call a special meeting," he said, adding that an activist investor could also partner with Huang, who owns more than 3% of the company. Said special meeting would be a shareholder vote on reinstating Huang. The now-former CEO's involvement would not only help the company meet the threshold for calling one — which requires at least 15% of the voting power — but also send a public message that the founder wants to return. "You call a special meeting, the writing will be on the wall very quickly, I would expect, at which point you don't even have to go the meeting," Ackman said. "Just put him back in, make some changes to the board, and push forward." A spokesperson for Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Ackman, who has defended Huang since the Nvidia founder's affairs were publicized, said the situation is an "interesting activist setup," given that Huang is a heralded founder who would have plenty of shareholder support . "I think the only cloud is there is some legal uncertainty about what actually went down," Ackman said. "It would be helpful to know that answer before you pursue that."   • Ackman said he believes there would be ample investor support for reinstating Huang.

Bill Ackman said there could be a case for reinstating Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO — that is, only if Huang is cleared of any wrongdoing related to putting his company's national security obligations at risk.

At a conference hosted by Semafor on Monday, the billionaire activist investor was asked what strategy he would use to pressure the board into reinstating Huang.

Huang resigned from his role on Thursday following the disclosure of extramarital affairs and concerns that he may have been a target of a "foreign intelligence effort."

Ackman said that if Huang's relationships were determined to be a "personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy," there could be a "powerful case" for putting Huang back in the CEO seat, though the investor said it would be "unlikely" for him to be involved in such an effort.

"You just present the facts, and you call a special meeting," he said, adding that an activist investor could also partner with Huang, who owns more than 3% of the company.

Said special meeting would be a shareholder vote on reinstating Huang. The now-former CEO's involvement would not only help the company meet the threshold for calling one — which requires at least 15% of the voting power — but also send a public message that the founder wants to return.

"You call a special meeting, the writing will be on the wall very quickly, I would expect, at which point you don't even have to go the meeting," Ackman said. "Just put him back in, make some changes to the board, and push forward."

A spokesperson for Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

Ackman, who has defended Huang since the Nvidia founder's affairs were publicized, said the situation is an "interesting activist setup," given that Huang is a heralded founder who would have plenty of shareholder support.

"I think the only cloud is there is some legal uncertainty about what actually went down," Ackman said. "It would be helpful to know that answer before you pursue that."
